Although the Hamiltonian vanishes, the theory is still not trivial because one must solve the constraint which follows by varying a0a_{0}. For the sake of concreteness, we will specialize to the case G=G=SU(2). Then the constraint reads:

ϵi​j​∂iaja¯+fa¯​b¯​c¯​a1b¯​a2c¯=0\epsilon_{ij}{\partial_{i}}{a_{j}^{\underline{a}}}+f^{{\underline{a}}\,{\underline{b}}\,{\underline{c}}}{a_{1}^{\underline{b}}}{a_{2}^{\underline{c}}}=0 (29)

where i,j=1,2i,j=1,2. The left-hand side of this equation is the field strength of the gauge field aia¯a_{i}^{\underline{a}}, where a¯=1,2,3{\underline{a}}=1,2,3 is an su(2) index. Since the field strength must vanish, we can always perform a gauge transformation so that aia¯=0a_{i}^{\underline{a}}=0 locally. Therefore this theory has no local degrees of freedom. However, for some field configurations satisfying the constraint, there may be a global topological obstruction which prevents us from making the gauge field zero everywhere. Clearly, this can only happen if Σ\Sigma is topologically non-trivial.

The simplest non-trivial manifold is the annulus, which is topologically equivalent to the sphere with two punctures. Following 86 (see also [338] for a similar construction on the torus), let us take coordinates (r,ϕ)(r,\phi) on the annulus, with r1<r<r2{r_{1}}<r<{r_{2}}, and let tt be time. Then we can write aμ=g​∂μg−1{a_{\mu}}=g{\partial_{\mu}}g^{-1}, where

g⁡(r,ϕ,t)=ei​ω​(r,ϕ,t)​ei​ϕk​λ​(t)g(r,\phi,t)=e^{i\omega(r,\phi,t)}\,e^{i\frac{\phi}{k}\lambda(t)} (30)

where ω⁡(r,ϕ,t)\omega(r,\phi,t) and λ⁡(t)\lambda(t) take values in the Lie algebra su(2) and ω⁡(r,ϕ,t)\omega(r,\phi,t) is a single-valued function of ϕ\phi. The functions ω\omega and λ\lambda are the dynamical variables of Chern-Simons theory on the annulus. Substituting (30) into the Chern-Simons action, we see that it now takes the form:

S=12​π​∫d​t​tr​(λ​∂tΩ)S=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int dt\,\text{tr}\left(\lambda{\partial_{t}}\Omega\right) (31)

where Ω⁡(r,t)=∫02​πd​ϕ​(ω⁡(r1,ϕ,t)−ω⁡(r2,ϕ,t))\Omega(r,t)=\int_{0}^{2\pi}d\phi\,(\omega({r_{1}},\phi,t)-\omega({r_{2}},\phi,t)). Therefore, Ω\Omega is canonically conjugate to λ\lambda. By a gauge transformation, we can always rotate λ\lambda and Ω\Omega so that they are along the 33 direction in su(2), i.e. λ=λ3​T3\lambda={\lambda_{3}}{T^{3}}, Ω=Ω3​T3\Omega={\Omega_{3}}{T^{3}}. Since it is defined through the exponential in (30), Ω3\Omega_{3} takes values in [0,2​π][0,2\pi]. Therefore, its canonical conjugate, λ3\lambda_{3}, is quantized to be an integer. From the definition of λ\lambda in (30), we see that λ3≡λ3+2​k{\lambda_{3}}\equiv{\lambda_{3}}+2k. However, by a gauge transformation given by a rotation around the 11-axis, we can transform λ→−λ\lambda\rightarrow-\lambda. Hence, the independent allowed values of λ\lambda are 0,1,…,k0,1,\ldots,k.

On the two-punctured sphere, if one puncture is of type aa, the other puncture must be of type a¯\bar{a}. (If the topological charge at one puncture is measured along a loop around the puncture – e.g. by a Wilson loop, see subsection III.3 – then the loop can be deformed so that it goes around the other puncture, but in the opposite direction. Therefore, the two punctures necessarily have conjugate topological charges.) For SU(2), a=a¯a=\bar{a}, so both punctures have the same topological charge. Therefore, the restriction to only k+1k+1 different possible allowed boundary conditions λ\lambda for the two-punctured sphere implies that there are k+1k+1 different quasiparticle types in SU(2)k Chern-Simons theory. As we will describe in later subsections, these allowed quasiparticle types can be identified with the j=0,12,…,k2j=0,\frac{1}{2},\ldots,\frac{k}{2} representations of the SU(2)2 Kac-Moody algebra.

III.1.2 TQFTs and Quasiparticle Properties

We will continue with our analysis of Chern-Simons theory in sections III.3 and III.4. Here, we will make some more general observations abut TQFTs and the topological properties of quasiparticles. We turn to the nn-punctured sphere, Σ=S2\P1∪P2∪…∪Pn\Sigma={S^{2}}\backslash{P_{1}}\cup{P_{2}}\cup\ldots\cup{P_{n}}, i.e. the sphere S2{S^{2}} with the points P1,P2​…​Pn{P_{1}},{P_{2}}\ldots{P_{n}} deleted, which is equivalent to n−1n-1 quasiparticles in the plane (the nthn^{\text{th}} puncture becomes the point at ∞\infty). This will allow us to study the topological properties of quasiparticle excitations purely from ground state properties. To see how braiding emerges in this approach, it is useful to note that diffeomorphisms should have a unitary representation on the ground state Hilbert space (i.e. they should commute with the Hamiltonian). Diffeomorphisms which can be smoothly deformed to the identity should have a trivial action on the Hilbert space of the theory since there are no local degrees of freedom. However, ‘large’ diffeomorphisms could have a non-trivial unitary representation on the theory’s Hilbert space. If we take the quotient of the diffeomorphism group by the set of diffeomorphisms which can be smoothly deformed to the identity, then we obtain the mapping class group. On the nn-punctured sphere, the braid group ℬn−1{\cal B}_{n-1} is a subgroup of the mapping class group.44 4 The mapping class group is non-trivial solely as a result of the punctures. In particular, any diffeomorphism which moves one or more of the punctures around other punctures cannot be deformed to the identity; conversely, if two diffeomorphisms move the same punctures along trajectories which can be deformed into each other, then the diffeomorphisms themselves can also be deformed into each other. These classes of diffeomorphisms correspond to the braid group which is, in fact, a normal subgroup. If we take the quotient of the mapping class group by the Dehn twists of n−1n-1 of the punctures – all except the point at infinity – we would be left with the braid group ℬn−1{\cal B}_{n-1}. Therefore, if we study Chern-Simons theory on the nn-punctured sphere as we did for the 22-punctured sphere above, and determine how the mapping class group acts, we can learn all of the desired information about quasiparticle braiding. We do this by two different methods in subsections III.3 and III.4.

One extra transformation in the mapping class group, compared to the braid group, is a 2​π2\pi rotation of a puncture/particle relative to the rest of the system (a Dehn twist). If we consider particles with a finite extent, rather than point particles, then we must consider the possibility of such rotations. For instance, if the particles are small dipoles, then we can represent their world lines as ribbons. A Dehn twist then corresponds to a twist of the ribbon. Thickening a world line into a ribbon is called a framing. A given world line has multiple choices of framing, corresponding to how many times the ribbon twists. A framing is actually essential in Chern-Simons theory because flux is attached to charge through the constraint (24) or (29). By putting the flux and charge at opposite edges of the ribbon, which is a short-distance regularization of the theory, we can associate a well-defined phase to a particle trajectory. Otherwise, we wouldn’t know how many times the charge went around the flux.

Any transformation acting on a single particle can only result in a phase; the corresponding phase is called the twist parameter Θa{\Theta_{a}}. Often, one writes Θa≡e2​π​i​ha{\Theta_{a}}\equiv e^{2\pi ih_{a}}, where hah_{a} is called the spin of the particle.55 5 If aa is its own anti-particle, so that two aas can fuse to 𝟏{\bf 1}, then R1a​a=±Θa∗{R^{aa}_{1}}=\pm{\Theta_{a}^{*}}, where the minus sign is acquired for some particle types aa which are not quite their own antiparticles but only up to some transformation which squares to −1-1. This is analogous to the fact that the fundamental representation of SU(2) is not real but is pseudoreal. Consequently, a spin-1/21/2 particle ψμ\psi_{\mu} and antiparticle ψμ†\psi^{\mu\dagger} can form a singlet, ψμ†ψμ\psi^{\mu\dagger}\psi_{\mu}, but two spin-1/21/2 particles can as well, ψμ​ψν​i​(σy)μ​ν{\psi_{\mu}}{\psi_{\nu}}i({\sigma_{y}})^{\mu\nu}, where σy\sigma_{y} is the antisymmetric Pauli matrix. When some quantities are computed, an extra factor of (i​σy)2=−1{({i\sigma_{y}})^{2}}=-1 results. This ±\pm sign is called the Froebenius-Schur indicator. (See, for instance, 22.) (One must, however, be careful to distinguish this from the actual spin of the particle, which determines its transformation properties under the three-dimensional rotation group and must be half-integral.) However, hah_{a} is well-defined even if the system is not rotationally-invariant, so it is usually called the topological spin of the particle. For Abelian anyons, it is just the statistics parameter, θ=2​π​i​ha\theta=2\pi ih_{a}.

The ground state properties on arbitrary surfaces, including the nn-punctured sphere and the torus, can be built up from more primitive vector spaces in the following way. An arbitrary closed surface can be divided into a collection of 33-punctured spheres which are glued together at their boundaries. This is called a ‘pants decomposition’ because of the topological equivalence of a 33-punctured sphere to a pair of pants. Therefore, the 33-punctured sphere plays a fundamental role in the description of a topological phase. Its Hilbert space is denoted by Va​bcV_{ab}^{c}, if aa, bb, and cc are the particle types at the three punctures. If the aa and bb punctures are fused, a two-punctured sphere will result. From the above analysis, it has a one-dimensional vector space if both punctures have topological charge cc and a zero-dimensional vector space otherwise. The dimension of the Hilbert space of the 33-punctured sphere is given by the fusion multiplicity Na​bc=dim​(Va​bc)N_{ab}^{c}=\text{dim}\left(V_{ab}^{c}\right) which appears in the fusion rule, ϕa×ϕb=∑cNa​bc​ϕc{\phi_{a}}\times{\phi_{b}}={\sum_{c}}{N_{ab}^{c}}{\phi_{c}}. The Hilbert space on a surface obtained by gluing together 33-punctured spheres is obtained by tensoring together the VV’s and summing over the particle types at the punctures where gluing occurs. For instance, the Hilbert space on the 44-punctured sphere is given by the direct sum Vea​b​d=⊕cVa​bcVc​deV^{e}_{abd}={\oplus_{c}}V_{ab}^{c}V_{cd}^{e}; the Hilbert space on the torus is VT2=⊕aV1​aaVa​1aV_{T^{2}}=\oplus_{a}V_{1a}^{a}V_{a1}^{a}. (If one of the particle types is the vacuum, then the corresponding puncture can simply be removed; the 33-punctured sphere is then actually only 22-punctured. Gluing two of them together end to end gives a torus. This is one way of seeing that the degeneracy on the torus is the number of particle types.)

The Hilbert space of the nn-punctured sphere with topological charge aa at each puncture can be constructed by sewing together a chain of (n−2)(n-2) 33-punctured spheres. The resulting Hilbert space is: V1a​…​a=⊕biVa​ab1Va​b1b2…Va​bN−3aV^{1}_{a\ldots a}={\oplus_{b_{i}}}V_{aa}^{b_{1}}V_{a{b_{1}}}^{b_{2}}\,\ldots\,V_{ab_{N-3}}^{a}. A simple graphical notation for a set of basis states of this Hilbert space is given by a fusion chain (similar to the fusion tree discussed in appendix A):

The first two aas on the far left fuse to b1b_{1}. The next aa fuses with b1b_{1} to give b2b_{2}. The next aa fuses with b2b_{2} to give b3b_{3}, and so on. The different basis vectors in this Hilbert space correspond to the different possible allowed bib_{i}s. The dimension of this Hilbert space is Na​ab1​Na​b1b2​…​Na​bN−3a=(Na)ab1​(Na)b1b2​…​(Na)bN−3aN_{aa}^{b_{1}}N_{a{b_{1}}}^{b_{2}}\,\ldots\,N_{ab_{N-3}}^{a}=\left({N_{a}}\right)_{a}^{b_{1}}\left({N_{a}}\right)_{{b_{1}}}^{b_{2}}\,\ldots\,\left({N_{a}}\right)_{b_{N-3}}^{a}. On the right-hand-side of this equation, we have suggested that the fusion multiplicity Na​bcN_{ab}^{c} can be viewed as a matrix (Na)bc\left({N_{a}}\right)_{b}^{c} associated with quasiparticle species aa. Let us denote the largest eigenvalue of the matrix Na{N_{a}} by dad_{a}. Then the Hilbert space of MM quasiparticles of type aa has dimension ∼daM−2\sim d_{a}^{M-2} for large MM. For this reason, dad_{a} is called the quantum dimension of an aa quasiparticle. It is the asymptotic degeneracy per particle of a collection of aa quasiparticle. For Abelian particles, da=1{d_{a}}=1 since the multi-particle Hilbert space is one-dimensional (for fixed particle positions). Non-Abelian particles have da>1{d_{a}}>1. Note that dad_{a} is not, in general, an integer, which is symptomatic of the non-locality of the Hilbert space: it is not the tensor product of dad_{a}-dimensional Hilbert spaces associated locally with each particle.

This non-locality is responsible for the stability of this degenerate ground state Hilbert space. Not only the Yang-Mills term, but all possible gauge-invariant terms which we can add to the action (26) are irrelevant. This means that adding such a term to the action might split the ∼daM−2\sim d_{a}^{M-2}-dimensional space of degenerate states in a finite-size system, but the splitting must vanish as the system size and the particle separations go to infinity. In fact, we can make an even stronger statement than that. All ground state matrix elements of gauge-invariant local operators such as the field strength squared, Fμ​νa¯​Fμ​ν​a¯F_{\mu\nu}^{\underline{a}}F^{\mu\nu{\underline{a}}}, vanish identically because of the Chern-Simons constraint. Therefore, the degeneracy is not lifted at all in perturbation theory. It can only be lifted by non-perturbative effects (e.g. instantons/quantum tunneling), which could cause a splitting ∼e−g​L\sim e^{-gL} where gg is inversely proportional to the coefficient of the Yang-Mills term. Therefore, the multi-quasiparticle states are degenerate to within exponential accuracy. At finite-temperatures, one must also consider transitions to excited states, but the contributions of these will be ∼e−Δ/T\sim e^{-\Delta/T}. Furthermore if we were to add a time dependent (source) term to the action, these properties will remain preserved so long as the frequency of this term remains small compared with the gap.

Aside from the nn-punctured spheres, the torus is the most important manifold for considering topological phases. Although not directly relevant to experiments, the torus is very important for numerical simulations since periodic boundary conditions are often the simplest choice. As noted above, the ground state degeneracy on the torus is equal to the number of quasiparticle species. Suppose one can numerically solve a Hamiltonian on the torus. If it has a gap between its ground state(s) and the lowest energy excited states, then its ground state degeneracy is an important topological property of the state – namely the number of of quasiparticle species. A simple physical understanding of this degeneracy can be obtained in the following way. Suppose that we have a system of electrons in a topological phase. If we consider the system on the torus, then the electrons must have periodic boundary conditions around either generator of the torus (i.e. around either handle), but the quasiparticles need not. In the Abelian ν=1/m\nu=1/m fractional quantum Hall state, for instance, it is possible for a quasiparticle to pick up a phase e2​π​i​n/me^{2\pi in/m} in going around the meridian of the torus, where nn can take any of the values n=0,1,…,m−1n=0,1,\ldots,m-1; electrons would still have periodic boundary conditions since they are made up of mm quasiparticles. Indeed, all mm of these possibilities occur, so the ground state is mm-fold degenerate.

Let us make this a little more precise. We introduce operators T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} which create a quasiparticle-quasihole pair, take the quasiparticle around the meridian or longitude, respectively, of the torus and annihilate them again. Then T1T_{1} and T2T_{2} must satisfy:

T2−1​T1−1​T2​T1=e2​π​i/mT_{2}^{-1}T_{1}^{-1}T_{2}T_{1}=e^{2\pi i/m} (32)

because T1−1​T1T_{1}^{-1}T_{1} amounts to a contractible quasiparticle-quasihole loop, as does T2−1​T2T_{2}^{-1}T_{2}; by alternating these processes, we cause these loops to be linked. The quasiparticle trajectories in spacetime (which can be visualized as a thickened torus) are equivalent to a simple link between two circles (the Hopf link): the first quasiparticle-quasihole pair is pulled apart along the meridian (T1T_{1}); but before they can be brought back together (T1−1T_{1}^{-1}), the second pair is pulled apart along the longitude (T2T_{2}). After the first pair is brought back together and annihilated (T1−1T_{1}^{-1}), the second one is, too (T2−1T_{2}^{-1}). In other words, the phase on the right-hand-side of Eq. 32 is simply the phase obtained when one quasiparticle winds around another. This algebra can be represented on a vector space of minimum dimension mm. Let us call the states in this vector space |n⟩|n\rangle, n=0,1,…,m−1n=0,1,\ldots,m-1. Then

T1​|n⟩\displaystyle{T_{1}}|n\rangle =\displaystyle= e2​π​i​n/m​|n⟩\displaystyle e^{2\pi in/m}|n\rangle (33)
T2​|n⟩\displaystyle{T_{2}}|n\rangle =\displaystyle= |(n+1)​ mod ​m⟩\displaystyle|(n+1)\text{ mod }m\rangle (34)

These mm states correspond to n=0,1,…,m−1n=0,1,\ldots,m-1 quanta of flux threaded through the torus. If we were to cut along a meridian and open the torus into an annulus, then these states would have flux nn threaded through the hole in the annulus and charge n/mn/m at the inner boundary of the annulus (and a compensating charge at the outer boundary). We can instead switch to a basis in which T2{T_{2}} is diagonal by a discrete Fourier transform. If we write |n~⟩=1m​∑n=0m−1e2​π​i​n​n~/m​|n⟩|{\tilde{n}}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\sum_{n=0}^{m-1}e^{2\pi in{\tilde{n}}/m}|n\rangle, then |n~⟩|{\tilde{n}}\rangle is an eigenstgate of T2T_{2} with eigenvalue e2​π​i​n~/me^{2\pi i{\tilde{n}}/m}. In this basis, T1T_{1} is an off-diagonal operator which changes the boundary conditions of quasiparticles around the longitude of the torus. In non-Abelian states, a more complicated version of the same thing occurs, as we discuss for the case of Ising anyons at the end of section III.2. The different boundary conditions around the meridian correspond to the different possible quasiparticle types which could thread the torus (or, equivalently, could be present at the inner boundary of the annulus if the torus were cut open along a meridian). One can switch to a basis in which the boundary conditions around the longitude are fixed. The desired basis change is analogous to the discrete Fourier transform given above and is given by the ‘SS-matrix’ or ‘modular SS-matrix’ of the theory. Switching the longitude and meridian is one of the generators of the mapping class group of the torus; the SS-matrix expresses how it acts on the ground state Hilbert space. The elements of the SS-matrix are closely related to quasiparticle braiding. By following a similar construction to the one with T1T_{1}, T2T_{2} above, one can see that Sa​bS_{ab} is equal to the amplitude for creating a​a¯a\bar{a} and b​b¯b\bar{b} pairs, braiding aa and bb, and annihilating again in pairs. This is why, in an Abelian state, the elements of the SS-matrix are all phases (up to an overall normalization which ensures unitarity), e.g. Sn​n′=1m​e2​π​i​n​n′/mS_{nn^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}e^{2\pi inn^{\prime}/m} in the example above. In a non-Abelian state, the different entries in the matrix can have different magnitudes, so the basis change is a little more complicated than a Fourier transform. Entries can even vanish in the non-Abelian case since, after aa and bb have been braided, aa and a¯\bar{a} may no longer fuse to 𝟏{\bf 1}.

In the case of Ising anyons on the torus (SU(2)2), there are three ground states. One basis is |𝟏m⟩|{{\bf 1}_{m}}\rangle, |σm⟩|{\sigma_{m}}\rangle, |ψm⟩|{\psi_{m}}\rangle, corresponding to the different allowed topological charges which would be measured at the inner boundary of the resulting annulus if the torus were cut open along its meridian. An equally good basis is given by eigenstates of topological charge around the longitude: |𝟏l⟩|{{\bf 1}_{l}}\rangle, |σl⟩|{\sigma_{l}}\rangle, |ψl⟩|{\psi_{l}}\rangle. As we will see in at the end of the next section, the basis change between them is given by

S=(121212120−1212−1212)\displaystyle S=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}\frac{1}{2}&\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}&\frac{1}{2}\\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}&0&-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\\ \frac{1}{2}&-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}&\frac{1}{2}\\ \end{array}\right)

The SS-matrix not only contains information about braiding, but also about fusion, according to Verlinde’s formula [324] (for a proof, see 234, 235):

Na​bc=∑xSa​x​Sb​x​Sc¯​xS𝟏​xN_{ab}^{c}={\sum_{x}}\frac{S_{ax}S_{bx}S_{\bar{c}x}}{S_{{\bf 1}x}} (39)

Consequently, the quantum dimension of a particle of species aa is:

da=S𝟏​aS𝟏𝟏{d_{a}}=\frac{S_{{\bf 1}a}}{S_{{\bf 11}}} (40)

The mathematical structure encapsulating these braiding and fusion rules is a modular tensor category [327, 322, 178, 16, 188]. A category is composed of objects and morphisms, which are maps between the objects which preserve their defining structure. The idea is that one can learn more about the objects by understanding the morphisms between them. In our case, the objects are particles with labels (which specify their species) as well as fixed configurations of several particles. The morphisms are particle trajectories, which map a set of labeled partices at some initial time to a set of labeled particles at some final time. A tensor category has a tensor product structure for multiplying objects; here, this is simply the fact that one can take two well-separated (and historically well-separated) collections of particles and consider their union to be a new ‘tensor-product’ collection. Since we consider particles in two dimensions, the trajectories are essentially the elements of the braid group, but they include the additional possibility of twisting. (Allowing twists in the strands of a braid yields a braided ribbon category.) We will further allow the trajectories to include the fusion of two particles (so that we now have a fusion category). Morphisms can, therefore, be defined by specifying Θa\Theta_{a}, Va​bcV_{ab}^{c}, RR, and FF.

Why is it necessary to invoke category theory simply to specify the topological properties of non-Abelian anyons? Could the braid group not be the highest level of abstraction that we need? The answer is that for a fixed number of particles nn, the braid group ℬn{\cal B}_{n} completely specifies their topological properties (perhaps with the addition of twists Θa\Theta_{a} to account for the finite size of the particles). However, we need representations of ℬn{\cal B}_{n} for all values of nn which are compatible with each other and with fusion (of which pair creation and annihilation is simply the special case of fusion to the vacuum). So we really need a more complex – and much more tightly constrained – structure. This is provided by the concept of a modular tensor category. The FF and RR matrices play particularly important roles. The FF matrix can essentially be viewed an associativity relation for fusion: we could first fuse ii with jj, and then fuse the result with kk; or we could fuse ii with the result of fusing jj with kk. The consistency of this property leads to a constraint on the FF-matrices called the pentagon equation. (An explicit example of the pentagon equation is worked out in Section IV.2.) Consistency between FF and RR leads to a constraint called the hexagon equation. Modularity is the condition that the SS-matrix be invertible. These self-consistency conditions are sufficiently strong that a solution to them completely defines a topological phase.66 6 Modulo details regarding the central charge cc at the edge. e2​π​i​c/8e^{2\pi ic/8} can be obtained from the topological spins, but not cc itself.

An equivalent alternative to studying punctured surfaces is to add non-dynamical charges which are coupled to the Chern-Simons gauge field. Then the right-hand-side of the constraint (29) is modified and a non-trivial gauge field configuration is again obtained which is essentially equivalent to that obtained around a puncture. In the following subsections, we will discuss the Hilbert spaces of SU(2)k Chern-Simons theory, either on the nn-punctured sphere or in the presence of non-dynamical sources. These discussions will enable us to compute the braiding and fusion matrices. The non-trivial quasiparticle of SU(2)1 is actually Abelian so we do not discuss this ‘trivial’ case. The next case, SU(2)2, is non-Abelian and may be relevant to the ν=5/2\nu=5/2 fractional quantum Hall state. It can be understood in several different equivalent ways, which express its underlying free Majorana fermion structure. Quantum computation with Majorana fermions is described in Section IV.1. In the next section, we explain this structure from the perspective of a superconductor with p+i​pp+ip pairing symmetry. Although this description is very elegant, it cannot be generalized to higher kk. Therefore, in the two sections after that, we describe two different approaches to solving SU(2)k Chern-Simons theory for general kk. We recapitulate the case of SU(2)2 in these other languages and also describe the case of SU(2)3. The latter has quasiparticles in its spectrum which are Fibonacci anyons, a particularly beautiful non-Abelian anyonic structure which allows for universal topological quantum computation. It may also underlie the observed ν=12/5\nu=12/5 fractonal quantum Hall state. More details of the Fibonacci theory are given in Sections IV.2.

III.2 Superconductors with p+i​pp+ip pairing symmetry

In this section, we will discuss the topological properties of a superconductor with p+i​pp+ip pairing symmetry following the method introduced by Read and Green [268]. This is the most elementary way in which a non-Abelian topological state can emerge as the ground state of a many-body system. This non-Abelian topological state has several possible realizations in various two dimensional systems: p+i​pp+ip superconductors, such as Sr2RuO4 (although the non-Abelian quasiparticles are half-quantum vortices in this case [67]); p+i​pp+ip superfluids of cold atoms in optical traps [148, 313], and the A-phase (especially the A1A_{1} phase[208, 326]) of 3He films; and the Moore-Read Pfaffian quantum Hall state [233]. The last of these is a quantum Hall incarnation of this state: electrons at filling fraction ν=1/2\nu=1/2 are equivalent to fermions in zero field interacting with an Abelian Chern-Simons gauge field. When the fermions pair and condense in a p+i​pp+ip superconducting state, the Pfaffian quantum Hall state forms [143]. Such a state can occur at 52=2+12\frac{5}{2}=2+\frac{1}{2} if the lowest Landau level (of both spins) is filled and inert, and the first excited Landau level is half-filled.

Ordinarily, one makes a distinction between the fermionic quasiparticles (or Bogoliubov-De Gennes quasiparticles) of a superconductor and vortices in a superconductor. This is because, in terms of electron variables, the former are relatively simple while the latter are rather complicated. Furthermore, the energy and length scales associated with the two are very different in the weak-coupling limit. However, fermionic quasiparticles and vortices are really just different types of quasiparticle excitations in a superconductor – i.e. different types of localized disturbances above the ground state. Therefore, we will often refer to them both as simply quasiparticles and use the terms Bogoliubov-de Gennes or fermionic when referring to the former. In a p+i​pp+ip superconductor, the quasiparticles which exhibit non-Abelian statistics are flux h​c/2​ehc/2e vortices.

III.2.1 Vortices and Fermion Zero Modes

Let us suppose that we have a system of fully spin-polarized electrons in a superconducting state of px+i​pyp_{x}+ip_{y} pairing symmetry. The mean field Hamiltonian for such a superconductor is,

H\displaystyle H =∫d​𝐫​ψ†​(𝐫)​h0​ψ​(𝐫)\displaystyle=\int\!\!\mathrm{d}{\bf r}\,\psi^{\dagger}({\bf r})h_{0}\psi({\bf r}) (41)

with single-particle term h0=−12​m​∇2−μ{h_{0}}=-\frac{1}{2m}{\nabla^{2}}-\mu and complex pp-wave pairing function

D(𝐫,𝐫′)=Δ(𝐫+𝐫′2)(i∂x′−∂y′)δ(𝐫−𝐫′).D({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime})=\Delta\!\left({\frac{{\bf r}+{\bf r^{\prime}}}{2}}\right)(i\partial_{x^{\prime}}-\partial_{y^{\prime}})\delta({\bf r}-{\bf r^{\prime}}). (42)

The Hamiltonian then takes the form:

H=E0+∑EE​ΓE†​ΓEH=E_{0}+\sum_{E}E\,\Gamma_{E}^{\dagger}\Gamma_{E} (51)

where ΓE†≡∫d​r​[uE​(𝐫)​ψ​(𝐫)+vE​(𝐫)​ψ†​(𝐫)]\Gamma_{E}^{\dagger}\equiv\int dr\left[u_{E}({\bf r})\psi({\bf r})+v_{E}({\bf r})\psi^{\dagger}({\bf r})\right] is the creation operator formed by the positive energy solutions of the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations and E0E_{0} is the ground state energy. For the ground state of the Hamiltonian (41) to be degenerate in the presence of several vortices (which are the most interesting quasiparticles in this theory) it is essential that the BdG equations have solutions with eigenvalue zero in this situation.

Before searching for zero eigenvalues of (III.2.1) in the presence of vortices, however, we focus on a uniform superconductor, where Δ\Delta is a constant. Read and Green [268] retain only the potential part of h0h_{0}, which for a uniform superconductor is a constant −μ-\mu. With this simplification, a BdG eigenstate with momentum kk has energy

Ek=μ2+Δ2​|k|2E_{k}=\sqrt{\mu^{2}+{\Delta^{2}}|k|^{2}} (52)

The ground state of (41) is the celebrated BCS wave function, written here in an un-normalized form,

|g.s.⟩=∏𝐤(1+v𝐤u𝐤c𝐤†c−𝐤†)|vac⟩=e∑𝐤v𝐤u𝐤​c𝐤†​c−𝐤†|vac⟩|{\rm g.s.}\rangle=\prod_{\bf k}\left(1+\frac{v_{\bf k}}{u_{\bf k}}c_{\bf k}^{\dagger}c_{\bf-k}^{\dagger}\right)|{\rm vac}\rangle=e^{\sum_{\bf k}\frac{v_{\bf k}}{u_{\bf k}}c_{\bf k}^{\dagger}c_{\bf-k}^{\dagger}}|{\rm vac}\rangle (53)

where

(|u𝐤|2|v𝐤|2)=12​(1∓μμ2+|Δ​k|2)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}|u_{\bf k}|^{2}\\ |v_{\bf k}|^{2}\end{array}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left(1\mp\frac{\mu}{\sqrt{\mu^{2}+|\Delta k|^{2}}}\right) (54)

are the BCS coherence factors. The wave function (53) describes a coherent state of an undetermined number of Cooper pairs, each in an internal state of angular momentum ℓ=−1\ell=-1. Its projection onto a fixed even number of particles NN is carried out by expanding the exponent in (53) to the (N/2)th(N/2)^{\text{th}} order. When written in first quantized language, this wave function describes a properly anti-symmetrized wave function of N/2N/2 Cooper-pairs, each in an internal state

g⁡(𝐫)=∑𝐤v𝐤u𝐤​ei​𝐤𝐫g({\bf r})=\sum_{\bf k}\frac{v_{\bf k}}{u_{\bf k}}e^{i{\bf k}{\bf r}} (55)

In first quantized form the multiparticle BCS wavefunction is then of the form of the Pfaffian of an antisymmetric matrix whose i−ji-j element is g⁡(𝐫i−𝐫j)g({{\bf r}_{i}}-{{\bf r}_{j}}), an antisymmetrized product of pair wavefunctions
