=\displaystyle= 𝒜⁡[g⁡(𝐫1−𝐫2)​g​(𝐫3−𝐫4)​…​g​(𝐫N−1−𝐫N)]\displaystyle{\cal A}\left[g({\bf r}_{1}-{\bf r}_{2})g({\bf r}_{3}-{\bf r}_{4})\ldots g({\bf r}_{N-1}-{\bf r}_{N})\right]

with 𝒜{\cal A} being an antisymmetrization operator.

The function g⁡(𝐫)g({\bf r}) depends crucially on the sign of μ\mu, since the small kk behavior of v𝐤/u𝐤v_{\bf k}/u_{\bf k} depends on that sign. When μ>0\mu>0, we have g⁡(r)=1/(x+i​y)g(r)=1/(x+iy) in the long distance limit [268]. If we assume this form holds for all distances, the Pfaffian wave function obtained is identical to the Moore-Read form discussed below in connection with the Ising model and the ν=5/2\nu=5/2 quantum Hall state in section III.4 (see Eqs. ). The slow decay of g⁡(r)g(r) implies a weak Cooper pairing. (But it does not imply that the state is gapless. One can verify that electron Green functions all decay exponentially for any non-zero μ\mu.) When μ<0\mu<0 the function g⁡(r)g(r) decays much more rapidly with rr, generically in an exponential way, such that the Cooper pairs are strongly bound. Furthermore, there is a topological distinction between the μ>0\mu>0 and μ<0\mu<0 phases. The distinction, which is discussed in detail in [268], implies that, despite the fact that both states are superconducting, the μ>0\mu>0 and μ<0\mu<0 states must be separated by a phase transition. (In the analogous quantum Hall state, both states are characterized by the same Hall conductivity but are separated by a phase transition, and are distinguished by their thermal Hall conductivities[268]) Indeed, from (52) we see that the gap vanishes for a uniform p+i​pp+ip superconductor with μ=0\mu=0. The low-energy BdG eigenstates at this second-order phase transition point form a Dirac cone.

For every solution (u,v)(u,v) of the BdG equations with energy EE, there is a solution (v∗,u∗)(v^{*},u^{*}) of energy −E-E. A solution with u=v∗u=v^{*} therefore has energy zero. We will soon be considering situations in which there are multiple zero energy solutions (ui,ui∗)({u_{i}},{u_{i}^{*}}), i=1,2,…i=1,2,\ldots. If we denote the corresponding operators by γi\gamma_{i} (see eq. 60 below), then they satisfy:

γi†=γi\gamma_{i}^{\dagger}=\gamma_{i} (57)

Eq. (57) is the definition of a Majorana fermion operator.

Let us now consider the BdG equations in the presence of vortices when the bulk of the superconductor is in the μ>0\mu>0 phase. As usual, a vortex is characterized by a point of vanishing Δ\Delta, and a 2​π2\pi-winding of the phase of Δ\Delta around that point. In principle we should, then, solve the BdG equations in the presence of such a non-uniform Δ\Delta. However, we can, instead, solve them in the presence of a non-uniform μ\mu, which is much simpler. All that we really need is to make the core of the superconductor topologically distinct from the bulk – i.e. a puncture in the superconductivity. Making μ<0\mu<0 in the core is just as good as taking Δ\Delta to zero, as far as topological properties are concerned. Therefore, we associate the core of the vortex with a region of μ<0\mu<0, whereas the bulk is at μ>0\mu>0. Thus, there is a μ=0\mu=0 line encircling the vortex core. This line is an internal edge of the system. We will consider the dynamics of edge excitations in more detail in section III.5, but here we will be content to show that a zero energy mode is among them.

The simplest situation to consider is that of azymuthal symmetry, with the polar coordinates denoted by rr and θ\theta. Imagine the vortex core to be at the origin, so that Δ⁡(r,θ)=|Δ⁡(r)|​ei​θ+i​Ω\Delta(r,\theta)=|\Delta(r)|e^{i\theta+i\Omega}. Here Ω\Omega is the phase of the order parameter along the θ=0\theta=0 line, a phase which will play an important role later in our discussion. Assume that the μ=0\mu=0 line is the circle r=r0r=r_{0}, and write

μ⁡(r)=Δ​h​(r),\mu(r)=\Delta\,h(r), (58)

with h⁡(r)h(r) large and positive for large r, and h⁡(r)<0h(r)<0 for r<r0r<{r_{0}}; therefore, the electron density will vanish for r≪r0r\ll{r_{0}}. Such a potential defines an edge at r=r0r={r_{0}}. There are low-energy eigenstates of the BdG Hamiltonian which are spatially localized near r=0r=0 and are exponentially decaying for r→∞r\rightarrow\infty:

ϕEe​d​g​e(r,θ)=ei​ℓ​θe−∫0rh(r′)dr′(e−iθ/2ei​θ/2),\phi^{edge}_{E}(r,\theta)=e^{i\ell\theta}e^{-\int_{0}^{r}h(r^{\prime})dr^{\prime}}\,{e^{-i\theta/2}\choose e^{i\theta/2}}, (59)

The spinor on the right-hand-side points in a direction in pseudospin space which is tangent to the r=r0r={r_{0}} circle at θ\theta. This wavefunction describes a chiral wave propagating around the edge, with angular momentum ℓ\ell and energy E=Δ​ℓ/r0E=\Delta\ell/{r_{0}}. Since the flux is an odd multiple of h​c/2​ehc/2e, the Bogoliubov quasiparticle (59) must be anti-periodic as it goes around the vortex. However, the spinor on the right-hand-side of (59) is also anti-periodic. Therefore, the angular momentum ℓ\ell must be an integer, ℓ∈ℤ\ell\in\mathbb{Z}. Consequently, a flux h​c/2​ehc/2e vortex has an ℓ=0\ell=0 solution, with energy E=0E=0. (Conversely, if the flux through the vortex were an even multiple of h​c/2​ehc/2e, ℓ\ell would be a half-integer, ℓ∈ℤ+12\ell\in\mathbb{Z}+\frac{1}{2}, and there would be no zero-mode.) The operator corresponding to this zero mode, which we will call γ\gamma, can be written in the form:

γ=12​∫d​r​[F⁡(𝐫)​e−i2​Ω​ψ​(𝐫)+F∗​(𝐫)​ei2​Ω​ψ†​(𝐫)]\gamma=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int dr\,\left[F({\bf r})\,e^{-\frac{i}{2}\Omega}\psi({\bf r})+\,F^{*}({\bf r})\,e^{\frac{i}{2}\Omega}\psi^{\dagger}({\bf r})\right] (60)

Here, F(𝐫)=e−∫0rh(r′)dr′e−iθ/2F({\bf r})=e^{-\int_{0}^{r}h(r^{\prime})dr^{\prime}}e^{-i\theta/2}. Since each γ\gamma is an equal superposition of electron and hole, it is overall a chargeless, neutral fermion operator

When there are several well separated vortices at positions 𝐑i{\bf R}_{i}, the gap function near the ithi^{\text{th}} vortex takes the form Δ⁡(𝐫)=|Δ⁡(𝐫)|​exp⁡(i​θi+i​Ωi)\Delta({\bf r})=|\Delta({\bf r})|\exp{(i\theta_{i}+i\Omega_{i})}, with θi=arg⁡(𝐫−𝐑𝐢)\theta_{i}=\arg{({\bf r}-{\bf R_{i}})} and Ωi=∑j≠iarg⁡((𝐑𝐣−𝐑i))\Omega_{i}=\sum_{j\neq i}\arg(({\bf R_{j}}-{\bf R}_{i})). There is then one zero energy solution per vortex. Each zero energy solution γi\gamma_{i} is localized near the core of its vortex at 𝐑𝐢{\bf R_{i}}, but the phase Ωi\Omega_{i} that replaces Ω\Omega in (60) depends on the position of all vortices. Moreover, the dependence of the Majorana operators γi\gamma_{i} on the positions 𝐑𝐢{\bf R_{i}} is not single valued.

While for any E≠0E\neq 0 the operators ΓE†,ΓE\Gamma_{E}^{\dagger},\Gamma_{E} are conventional fermionic creation and annihilation operators, the γi\gamma_{i}’s are not. In particular, for E≠0E\neq 0 we have (ΓE†)2=ΓE2=0(\Gamma_{E}^{\dagger})^{2}=\Gamma_{E}^{2}=0, but the zero energy operators follow (with a convenient choice of normalization) γi2=1\gamma_{i}^{2}=1. The two types of fermion operator share the property of mutual anti-commutation, i.e., the γ\gamma’s satisfy {γi,γj}=2​δi​j\{\gamma_{i},\gamma_{j}\}=2\delta_{ij}.

III.2.2 Topological Properties of p+i​pp+ip Superconductors

The existence of the γi\gamma_{i}’s implies a degeneracy of the ground state. The counting of the number of degenerate ground states should be done with care. A pair of conventional fermionic creation and annihilation operators span a two dimensional Hilbert space, since their square vanishes. This is not true for a Majorana operator. Thus, to count the degeneracy of the ground state when 2​N02N_{0} vortices are present, we construct “conventional” complex (Dirac) fermionic creation and annihilation operators,

ψi=(γi+i​γN0+i)/2\displaystyle\psi_{i}=(\gamma_{i}+i\gamma_{N_{0}+i})/2 (61)
ψi†=(γi−i​γN0+i)/2\displaystyle\psi_{i}^{\dagger}=(\gamma_{i}-i\gamma_{N_{0}+i})/2 (62)

These operators satisfy ψi2=(ψi†)2=0\psi_{i}^{2}=\left(\psi_{i}^{\dagger}\right)^{2}=0 and thus span a two-dimensional subspace of degenerate ground states associated with these operators. Over all, then, the system has 2N02^{N_{0}} degenerate ground states. If the fermion number is fixed to be even or odd, then the degeneracy is 2N0−12^{{N_{0}}-1}. Therefore, the quantum dimension of a vortex is dvort=2d_{\rm vort}=\sqrt{2} or, in the notation introduced in Sec. II.1.1 for Ising anyons, dσ=2{d_{\sigma}}=\sqrt{2}.

For any two vortices ii and jj, we can associate a two state system. If we work in the basis of i​γi​γji{\gamma_{i}}{\gamma_{j}} eigenstates, then i​γi​γji{\gamma_{i}}{\gamma_{j}} acts as σz\sigma_{z} with eigenvalues ±1\pm 1, while γi\gamma_{i} and γj\gamma_{j} act as σx\sigma_{x} and σy\sigma_{y}. (However, it is important to keep in mind that Majorana fermions γk\gamma_{k}, γl\gamma_{l} anti-commute with γi\gamma_{i}, γj\gamma_{j}, unlike operators associated with different spins, which commute.) The two eigenvalues i​γi​γj=∓1i{\gamma_{i}}{\gamma_{j}}=\mp 1 are the two fusion channels of two fermions. If we form the Dirac fermion ψ=(γi+i​γj)/2\psi=({\gamma_{i}}+i{\gamma_{j}})/2, then the two i​γi​γji{\gamma_{i}}{\gamma_{j}} eigenstates have ψ†​ψ=0,1{\psi^{\dagger}}\psi=0,1. Therefore, we will call these fusion channels 𝟏{\bf 1} and ψ\psi. (One is then tempted to refer to the state for which ψ†​ψ=1\psi^{\dagger}\psi=1 as a “filled fermion”, and to the ψ†​ψ=0\psi^{\dagger}\psi=0 state as an empty fermion. Note however that the eigenvalue of ψ†​ψ\psi^{\dagger}\psi has no bearing on the occupation of single-particle states.)

Of course, the pairing of vortices to form Dirac fermions is arbitrary. A given pairing defines a basis, but one can transform to a basis associated with another pairing. Consider four vortices with corresponding zero modes γ1\gamma_{1}, γ2\gamma_{2}, γ3\gamma_{3}, γ4\gamma_{4}. The FF-matrix transforms states from the basis in which i​γ1​γ2i{\gamma_{1}}{\gamma_{2}} and i​γ3​γ4i{\gamma_{3}}{\gamma_{4}} are diagonal to the basis in which i​γ1​γ4i{\gamma_{1}}{\gamma_{4}} and i​γ2​γ3i{\gamma_{2}}{\gamma_{3}} are diagonal. Since i​γ1​γ4i{\gamma_{1}}{\gamma_{4}} acts as σx\sigma_{x} on an i​γ1​γ2i{\gamma_{1}}{\gamma_{2}} eigenstate, the FF-matrix is just the basis change from the σz\sigma_{z} basis to the σx\sigma_{x} basis:

[Fσσ​σ​σ]=12​(111−1)\displaystyle\left[F^{\sigma\sigma\sigma}_{\sigma}\right]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}1&1\\ 1&-1\\ \end{array}\right)

We will refer to this type of non-Abelian anyons by the name ‘Ising anyons’; they are the model introduced in Section II.1.1. The reason for the name will be explained in Section III.5.

In a compact geometry, there must be an even number of vortices (since a vortex carries half a flux quantum, and the number of flux quanta penetrating a compact surface must be integer). In a non-compact geometry, if the number of vortices is odd, the edge has a zero energy state of its own, as we show in Section III.5.

Now, let us examine what happens to the Majorana operators and to the ground states as vortices move. The positions of the vortices are parameters in the Hamiltonian (41). When they vary adiabatically in time, the operators γi\gamma_{i} vary adiabatically in time. In principle, there are two sources for this variation - the explicit dependence of γi\gamma_{i} on the positions and the Berry phase associated with the motion. The choice of phases taken at (60) is such that the Berry phase vanishes, and the entire time dependence is explicit. The non-single-valuedness of the phases in (60) implies then that a change of 2​π2\pi in Ω\Omega, which takes place when one vortex encircles another, does not leave the state unchanged.

As vortices adiabatically traverse trajectories that start and end in the same set of positions [166, 305], there is a unitary transformation UU within the subspace of ground states that takes the initial state |ψ⁡(t=0)⟩|\psi(t=0)\rangle to the final one |ψ⁡(t=T)⟩|\psi(t=T)\rangle,

|ψ⁡(t=T)⟩=U⁡|ψ⁡(t=0)⟩.|\psi(t=T)\rangle=U|\psi(t=0)\rangle. (66)

Correspondingly, the time evolution of the operators γi\gamma_{i} is

γi​(t=T)=U​γi​(t=0)​U†.\gamma_{i}(t=T)=U\gamma_{i}(t=0)U^{\dagger}. (67)

By reading the time evolution of γi\gamma_{i} from their explicit form (60) we can determine UU up to a phase. Indeed, one expects this Abelian phase to depend not only on the topology of the trajectory but also on its geometry, especially in the analogous quantum Hall case, where there is an Aharonov-Bohm phase accumulated as a result of the charge carried by the quasiparticle.

When vortex ii encircles vortex i+1i+1, the unitary transformation is simple: both γi\gamma_{i} and γi+1\gamma_{i+1} are multiplied by −1-1, with all other operators unchanged. This is a consequence of the fact that when the order parameter changes by a phase factor 2​π2\pi, fermionic operators change by a phase π\pi. Exchange trajectories, in which some of the vortices trade places, are more complicated, since the phase changes of Ωk\Omega_{k} associated with a particular trajectory do not only depend on the winding numbers, but also on the details of the trajectory and on the precise definition of the cut of the function arg⁡(𝐫)\arg({\bf r}) where its value jumps by 2​π2\pi.

The simplest example is the interchange of two vortices. Inevitably, one of the vortices crosses the branch cut line of the other vortex. We can place the branch cuts so that a counterclockwise exchange of vortices 11 and 22 transforms c1→c2c_{1}\rightarrow c_{2} and c2→−c1c_{2}\rightarrow-c_{1} while a clockwise exchange transforms c1→−c2c_{1}\rightarrow-c_{2} and c2→c1c_{2}\rightarrow c_{1} [166].

This may be summarized by writing the representation matrices for the braid group generators [247, 166]:

ρ⁡(σi)=ei​θ​e−π4​γi​γi+1\rho({\sigma_{i}})=e^{i\theta}\,e^{-\frac{\pi}{4}{\gamma_{i}}\gamma_{i+1}} (68)

where θ\theta is the Abelian part of the transformation. The two eigenvalues i​γi​γi+1=∓1i{\gamma_{i}}\gamma_{i+1}=\mp 1 are the two fusion channels 𝟏{\bf 1} and ψ\psi of a pair of vortices. From (68), we see that the RR-matrices satisfy Rψσ​σ=i​R𝟏σ​σR^{\sigma\sigma}_{\psi}=i\,R^{\sigma\sigma}_{\bf 1} (i.e., the phase of taking two σ\sigma particles around each other differ by ii depending on whether they fuse to ψ\psi or 𝟏{\bf 1}). It is difficult to obtain the Abelian part of the phase using the methods of this section, but we will derive it by other methods in Sections III.3 and III.4. The non-Abelian part of (68), i.e. the second factor on the right-hand-side, is the same as a π/2\pi/2 rotation in the spinor representation of SO(2n) (see 247 for details). The fact that braiding only enacts π/2\pi/2 rotations is the reason why this type of non-Abelian anyon does not enable universal topological quantum computation, as we discuss further in section IV.

According to (68), if a system starts in a ground state |gsα⟩\left|{\rm gs}_{\alpha}\right\rangle and vortex jj winds around vortex j+1j+1, the system’s final state is γjγj+1|gsα⟩\gamma_{j}\gamma_{j+1}\left|{\rm gs}_{\alpha}\right\rangle. Writing this out in terms of the original electron operators, we have

(cjei2​Ωj+cj†e−i2​Ωj)(cj+1ei2​Ωj+1+cj+1†e−i2​Ωj+1)|gsα⟩,\left(c_{j}e^{\frac{i}{2}\Omega_{j}}+c_{j}^{\dagger}e^{-\frac{i}{2}\Omega_{j}}\right)\left(c_{j+1}e^{\frac{i}{2}\Omega_{j+1}}+c_{j+1}^{\dagger}e^{-\frac{i}{2}\Omega_{j+1}}\right)\left|{\rm gs}_{\alpha}\right\rangle, (69)

where cj(†)c_{j}^{(\dagger)} annihilates a particle in the state F⁡(r−Rj)F(r-R_{j}) and cj+1(†)c_{j+1}^{(\dagger)} creates a particle in the state (F⁡(r−Rj+1)F(r-R_{j+1})) localized very close to the cores of the jjth and (j+1)(j+1)th vortex, respectively. Eq. (69) seemingly implies that the motion of the jjth vortex around the (j+1)(j+1)th vortex affects the occupations of states very close to the cores of the two vortices. This is in contrast, however, to the derivation leading to Eq. (69), which explicitly assumes that vortices are kept far enough from one another so that tunneling between vortex cores may be disregarded.

This seeming contradiction is analyzed in detail in 305, where it is shown that the unitary transformation (69) does not affect the occupation of the core states of the j,j+1j,j+1 vortices, because all ground states are composed of superpositions in which the core states have a probability of one-half to be occupied and one-half to be empty. The unitary transformation within the ground state subspace does not change that probability. Rather, they affect phases in the superpositions. Using this point of view it is then possible to show that two ingredients are essential for the non-Abelian statistics of the vortices. The first is the quantum entanglement of the occupation of states near the cores of distant vortices. The second ingredient is familiar from (Abelian) fractional statistics: the geometric phase accumulated by a vortex traversing a closed loop.

Therefore, we conclude that, for p−p-wave superconductors, the existence of zero-energy intra-vortex modes leads, first, to a multitude of ground states, and, second, to a particle-hole symmetric occupation of the vortex cores in all ground states. When represented in occupation-number basis, a ground state is a superposition which has equal probability for the vortex core being empty or occupied by one fermion. When a vortex traverses a trajectory that encircles another vortex, the phase it accumulates depends again on the number of fluid particles it encircles. Since a fluid particle is, in this case, a Cooper pair, the occupation of a vortex core by a fermion, half a pair, leads to an accumulation of a phase of π\pi relative to the case when the core is empty. And since the ground state is a superposition with equal weights for the two possibilities, the relative phase of π\pi introduced by the encircling might in this case transform the system from one ground state to another.

Now consider the ground state degeneracy of a p+i​pp+ip superconductor on the torus. Let us define, following 251 (see also 60), the operators A1A_{1}, A2A_{2} which create a pair of Bogoliubov-de Gennes quasiparticles, take one around the meridian or longitude of the torus, respectively, and annihilate them again. We then define B1B_{1}, B2B_{2} as operators which create a vortex-antivortex pair, take the vortex around the meridian or longitude of the torus, respectively, and annihilate them. B1B_{1} increases the flux through the hole encircled by the longitude of the torus by one half of a flux quantum while B2B_{2} does the same for the other hole. These operators satisfy the commutation relations [A1,A2]=0\left[{A_{1}},{A_{2}}\right]=0 and A1​B2=−B2​A1{A_{1}}{B_{2}}=-{B_{2}}{A_{1}}, A2​B1=−B1​A2{A_{2}}{B_{1}}=-{B_{1}}{A_{2}}. We can construct a multiplet of ground states as follows. Since A1{A_{1}} and A2{A_{2}} commute and square to 11, we can label states by their A1A_{1} and A2A_{2} eigenvalues ±1\pm 1. Let |1,1⟩|1,1\rangle be the state with both eigenvalues equal to 11, i.e. A1|1,1⟩=A2|1,1⟩=|1,1⟩{A_{1}}|1,1\rangle={A_{2}}|1,1\rangle=|1,1\rangle. Then B1|1,1⟩=|1,−1⟩{B_{1}}|1,1\rangle=|1,-1\rangle and B2|1,1⟩=|−1,1⟩{B_{2}}|1,1\rangle=|-1,1\rangle. Suppose we now try to apply B2{B_{2}} to B1|1,1⟩=|1,−1⟩{B_{1}}|1,1\rangle=|1,-1\rangle. This will create a vortex-antivortex pair; the Majorana zero modes, γa\gamma_{a}, γb\gamma_{b} associated with the vortex and anti-vortex will be in the state |0⟩|0\rangle defined by (γa+i​γb)​|0⟩=0\left({\gamma_{a}}+i{\gamma_{b}}\right)|0\rangle=0. When the vortex is taken around the longitude of the torus, its Majorana mode will be multiplied by −1-1: γa→−γa{\gamma_{a}}\rightarrow-{\gamma_{a}}. Now, the vortex-antivortex pair will no longer be in the state |0⟩|0\rangle, but will instead be in the state |1⟩|1\rangle defined by (γa−i​γb)​|1⟩=0\left({\gamma_{a}}-i{\gamma_{b}}\right)|1\rangle=0. Consequently, the vortex-antivortex pair can no longer annihilate to the vacuum. When they fuse, a fermion is left over. Therefore, B2B1|1,1⟩{B_{2}}{B_{1}}|1,1\rangle does not give a new ground state (and, by a similar argument, neither does B1B2|1,1⟩{B_{1}}{B_{2}}|1,1\rangle). Consequently, a p+i​pp+ip superconductor has ‘only’ three ground states on the torus. A basis in which B1B_{1} is diagonal is given by: (|1,1⟩±|1,−1⟩)/2(|1,1\rangle\pm|1,-1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}, with eigenvalue ±1\pm 1, and |−1,1⟩|-1,1\rangle, with eigenvalue 00 (since there is zero amplitude for B1|−1,1⟩{B_{1}}|-1,1\rangle to be in the ground state subspace). They can be identified with the states |1m⟩|{1_{m}}\rangle, |ψm⟩|{\psi_{m}}\rangle, and |σm⟩|{\sigma_{m}}\rangle in Ising anyon language. Meanwhile, B2{B_{2}} is diagonal in the basis (|1,1⟩±|−1,1⟩)/2(|1,1\rangle\pm|-1,1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}, |1,−1⟩|1,-1\rangle. By changing from one basis to the other, we find the SS-matrix given in the previous subsection follows.

The essential feature of chiral pp-wave superconductors is that they have Majorana fermion excitations which have zero energy modes at vortices (and gapless excitations at the edge of the system, see section III.5). The Majorana character is a result of the superconductivity, which mixes particle and hole states; the zero modes and gapless edge excitations result from the chirality. Majorana fermions arise in a completely different way in the Kitaev honeycomb lattice model [188]:

H=−Jx∑x−linksσxjσxj−Jy∑y−linksσyjσyj−Jz∑z−linksσxjσzjH=-{J_{x}}\sum_{x-\text{links}}{\sigma^{x}_{j}}{\sigma^{x}_{j}}-{J_{y}}\sum_{y-\text{links}}{\sigma^{y}_{j}}{\sigma^{y}_{j}}-{J_{z}}\sum_{z-\text{links}}{\sigma^{x}_{j}}{\sigma^{z}_{j}} (70)

where the zz-links are the vertical links on the honeycomb lattice, and the xx and yy links are at angles ±π/3\pm\pi/3 from the vertical. The spins can be represented by Majorana fermions bxb^{x}, byb^{y}, bzb^{z}, and cc, according to σjx=i​bjx​cj{\sigma^{x}_{j}}=i{b_{j}^{x}}{c_{j}}, σjx=i​bjy​cj{\sigma^{x}_{j}}=i{b_{j}^{y}}{c_{j}}, σjx=i​bjz​cj{\sigma^{x}_{j}}=i{b_{j}^{z}}{c_{j}} so long as the constraint bjx​bjy​bjz​cj=1{b_{j}^{x}}{b_{j}^{y}}{b_{j}^{z}}{c_{j}}=1 is satisfied. Then, the Hamiltonian is quartic in Majorana fermion operators, but the operators bjx​bkx{b_{j}^{x}}{b_{k}^{x}}, bjy​bky{b_{j}^{y}}{b_{k}^{y}}, bjz​bkz{b_{j}^{z}}{b_{k}^{z}} commute with the Hamiltonian. Therefore, we can take their eigenvalues as parameters uj​k=bjα​bkαu_{jk}={b_{j}^{\alpha}}{b_{k}^{\alpha}}, with α=x,y,\alpha=x,y, or zz appropriate to the j​kjk link. These parameters can be varied to minimize the Hamiltonian, which just describes Majorana fermions hopping on the honeycomb lattice:

H=i4​∑j​ktj​k​cj​ckH=\frac{i}{4}\sum_{jk}t_{jk}{c_{j}}{c_{k}} (71)

where tj​k=2​Jα​uj​kt_{jk}=2{J_{\alpha}}u_{jk} for nearest neighbor jj, kk and zero otherwise. For different values of the JαJ_{\alpha}s, the tj​kt_{jk}’s take different values. The topological properties of the corresponding cjc_{j} bands are encapsulated by their Chern number [188]. For a certain range of JαJ_{\alpha}s, a P,TP,T-violating perturbation gives the Majorana fermions a gap in such a way as to support zero modes on vortex-like excitations (plaquettes on which one of the uj​ku_{jk}s is reversed in sign). These excitations are identical in topological character to the vortices of a p+i​pp+ip superconductor discussed above.

III.3 Chern-Simons Effective Field Theories, the Jones Polynomial, and Non-Abelian Topological Phases

III.3.1 Chern-Simons Theory and Link Invariants

In the previous subsection, we have seen an extremely simple and transparent formulation of the quasiparticle braiding properties of a particular non-Abelian topological state which, as we will see later in this section, is equivalent to SU(2)2 Chern-Simons theory. It describes the multi-quasiparticle Hilbert space and the action of braiding operations in terms of free fermions. Most non-Abelian topological states are not so simple, however. In particular, SU(2)k Chern-Simons theory for k>2k>2 does not have a free fermion or boson description.77 7 It is an open question whether there is an alternative description of an SU(2)k topological phase with k>2k>2 in terms of fermions or bosons which is similar to the p+i​pp+ip chiral superconductor formulation of SU(2)2. Therefore, in the next two subsections, we discuss these field theories using more general methods.

Even though its Hamiltonian vanishes and it has no local degrees of freedom, solving Chern-Simons theory is still a non-trivial matter. The reason is that it is difficult in a non-Abelian gauge theory to disentangle the physical topological degrees of freedom from the unphysical local gauge degrees of freedom. There are essentially two approaches. Each has its advantages, and we will describe them both. One is to work entirely with gauge-invariant quantities and derive rules governing them; this is the route which we pursue in this subsection. The second is to pick a gauge and simply calculate within this gauge, which we do in the next subsection (III.4).

Consider SU(2)k non-Abelian Chern-Simons theory:

SC​S​[a]=k4​π​∫ℳtr⁡(a∧𝑑a+23​a∧a∧a)\displaystyle S_{CS}[a]=\frac{k}{4\pi}\int_{\cal M}{\rm tr}\left(a\wedge da+\frac{2}{3}a\wedge a\wedge a\right) (72)

We modify the action by the addition of sources, jμ​a¯j^{\mu{\underline{a}}}, according to ℒ→ℒ+tr⁡(j⋅a){\cal L}\rightarrow{\cal L}+{\rm tr}\left(j\cdot a\right). We take the sources to be a set of particles on prescribed classical trajectories. The ithi^{\text{th}} particle carries the spin jij_{i} representation of SU(2). As we saw in subsection III.1, there are only k+1k+1 allowed representations; later in this subsection, we will see that if we give a particle a higher spin representation than j=k/2j=k/2, then the amplitude will vanish identically. Therefore, jij_{i} must be in allowed set of k+1k+1 possibilities: 0,12,…,k20,\frac{1}{2},\ldots,\frac{k}{2}. The functional integral in the presence of these sources can be written in terms of Wilson loops, Wγi,ji​[a]{W_{{\gamma_{i}},{j_{i}}}}[a], which are defined as follows. The holonomy Uγ,j​[a]U_{\gamma,j}[a] is an S​U​(2)SU(2) matrix associated with a curve γ\gamma. It is defined as the path-ordered exponential integral of the gauge field along the path γ\gamma:

Uγ,j​[a]≡𝒫​ei​∮γ𝐚c¯​Tc¯⋅𝑑𝐥=∑n=0∞in∫02​πds1∫0s1ds2…∫0sn−1dsn[γ˙(s1)⋅𝐚a¯1(γ(s1))Ta¯1…γ˙(sn)⋅𝐚a¯n(γ(sn))Ta¯n]U_{\gamma,j}[a]\equiv{\cal P}{e^{i{\oint_{\gamma}}{{\bf a}^{\underline{c}}T^{\underline{c}}\cdot d{\bf l}}}}\\ ={\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}}{i^{n}}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}}\!\!{ds_{1}}{\int_{0}^{s_{1}}}\!\!{ds_{2}}\ldots{\int_{0}^{s_{n-1}}}\!\!{ds_{n}}\Bigl[\dot{\bf\gamma}({s_{1}})\cdot{{\bf a}^{{\underline{a}}_{1}}}\left({\bf\gamma}({s_{1}})\right){T^{{\underline{a}}_{1}}}\ldots\,\\ \dot{\bf\gamma}({s_{n}})\cdot{{\bf a}^{{\underline{a}}_{n}}}\left({\bf\gamma}({s_{n}})\right){T^{{\underline{a}}_{n}}}\Bigr] (73)

where 𝒫{\cal P} is the path-ordering symbol. The Lie algebra generators Ta¯T^{\underline{a}} are taken in the spin jj representation. γ→​(s)\vec{\gamma}(s), s∈[0,2​π]s\in[0,2\pi] is a parametrization of γ\gamma; the holonomy is clearly independent of the parametrization. The Wilson loop is the trace of the holonomy:

Wγ,j​[a]=tr⁡(Uγ,j​[a]){W_{\gamma,j}}[a]={\rm tr}\left(U_{\gamma,j}[a]\right) (74)

Let us consider the simplest case, in which the source is a quasiparticle-quasihole pair of type jj which is created out of the ground state, propagated for a period of time, and then annihilated, returning the system to the ground state. The amplitude for such a process is given by:

⟨0|0⟩γ,j=∫𝒟​a​ei​SC​S​[a]​Wγ,j​[a]\left\langle 0|0\right\rangle_{\gamma,j}=\int{\cal D}a\,e^{iS_{CS}[a]}\,{W_{\gamma,j}}[a] (75)

Here, γ\gamma is the spacetime loop formed by the trajectory of the quasiparticle-quasihole pair. The Wilson loop was introduced as an order parameter for confinement in a gauge theory because this amplitude roughly measures the force between the quasiparticle and the quasihole. If they were to interact with a confining force V⁡(r)∼rV(r)\sim r, then the logarithm of this amplitude would be proportional to the the area of the loop; if they were to have a short-ranged interaction, it would be proportional to the perimeter of the loop. However, Chern-Simons theory is independent of a metric, so the amplitude cannot depend on any length scales. It must simply be a constant. For j=1/2j=1/2, we will call this constant dd. As the notation implies, it is, in fact, the quantum dimension of a j=1/2j=1/2 particle. As we will see below, dd can be determined in terms of the level kk, and the quantum dimensions of higher spin particles can be expressed in terms of dd.

We can also consider the amplitude for two pairs of quasiparticles to be created out of the ground state, propagated for some time, and then annihilated, returning the system to the ground state:

⟨0|0⟩γ1,j1;γ2,j2=∫𝒟​a​ei​SC​S​[a]​Wγ,j​[a]​Wγ′,j′​[a]\left\langle 0|0\right\rangle_{{\gamma_{1}},{j_{1}};{\gamma_{2}},{j_{2}}}=\int{\cal D}a\,e^{iS_{CS}[a]}\,{W_{{\gamma},{j}}}[a]\,{W_{{\gamma^{\prime}},{j^{\prime}}}}[a] (76)

This amplitude can take different values depending on how γ\gamma and γ′\gamma^{\prime} are linked as in Fig. 4a vs 4b. If the curves are unlinked the integral must give d2d^{2}, but when they are linked the value can be nontrivial. In a similar way, we can formulate the amplitudes for an arbitrary number of sources.

It is useful to think about the history in figure 4a as a two step process: from t=−∞t=-\infty to t=0t=0 and from t=0t=0 to t=∞t=\infty. (The two pairs are created at some time t<0t<0 and annihilated at some time t>0t>0.) At t=0−t=0^{-}, the system is in a four-quasiparticle state. (Quasiparticles and quasiholes are topologically equivalent if G=G=SU(2), so we will use ‘quasiparticle’ to refer to both.) Let us call this state ψ\psi:

ψ[A]=∫a⁡(𝐱,0)=A⁡(𝐱)𝒟a(𝐱,t)Wγ−,j[a]Wγ−′,j′[a]×e∫−∞0d​t​∫d2​x​ℒCS\psi[A]=\int_{a({\bf x},0)=A({\bf x})}\!\!\!\!{\cal D}a({\bf x},t)\>W_{{\gamma_{-}},j}[a]\>W_{{\gamma^{\prime}_{-}},j^{\prime}}[a]\,\times\\ e^{{\int_{-\infty}^{0}}dt\int{d^{2}}x\>{\cal L}_{\rm CS}} (77)

where γ−{\gamma_{-}} and γ−′{\gamma^{\prime}_{-}} are the arcs given by γ⁡(t)\gamma(t) and γ′​(t)\gamma^{\prime}(t) for t<0t<0. A⁡(𝐱)A({\bf x}) is the value of the gauge field on the t=0t=0 spatial slice; the wavefunctional ψ⁡[A]\psi[A] assigns an amplitude to every spatial gauge field configuration. For GG=SU(2) and k>1k>1, there are actually two different four-quasiparticle states: if particles 11 and 22 fuse to the identity field j=0j=0, then particles 33 and 44 must as well; if particles 11 and 22 fuse to j=1j=1, then particles 33 and 44 must as well. These are the only possibilities. (For k=1k=1, fusion to j=1j=1 is not possible.) Which one the system is in depends on how the trajectories of the four quasiparticles are intertwined. Although quasiparticles 11 and 22 were created as a pair from the vacuum, quasiparticle 22 braided with quasiparticle 33, so 11 and 22 may no longer fuse to the vacuum. In just a moment, we will see an example of a different four-quasiparticle state.

We now interpret the t=0t=0 to t=∞t=\infty history as the conjugate of a t=−∞t=-\infty to t=0t=0 history. In other words, it gives us a four quasiparticle bra rather than a four quasiparticle ket:

χ∗[A]=∫a⁡(𝐱,0)=A⁡(𝐱)𝒟a(𝐱,t)Wγ+,j[a]Wγ+′,j′[a]×e∫0∞d​t​∫d2​x​ℒCS{\chi^{*}}[A]=\int_{a({\bf x},0)=A({\bf x})}\!\!\!\!{\cal D}a({\bf x},t)\>W_{{\gamma_{+}},j}[a]\>W_{{\gamma^{\prime}_{+}},j^{\prime}}[a]\,\times\\ e^{{\int_{0}^{\infty}}dt\int{d^{2}}x\>{\cal L}_{\rm CS}} (78)

In the state |χ⟩|\chi\rangle, quasiparticles 11 and 22 fuse to form the trivial quasiparticle, as do quasiparticles 33 and 44. Then we can interpret the functional integral from t=−∞t=-\infty to t=∞t=\infty as the matrix element between the bra and the ket:

⟨χ|ψ⟩=∫𝒟​a​ei​SC​S​[a]​Wγ1,j1​[a]​Wγ2,j2​[a]\langle\chi|\psi\rangle=\int{\cal D}a\,e^{iS_{CS}[a]}\,{W_{{\gamma_{1}},{j_{1}}}}[a]\,{W_{{\gamma_{2}},{j_{2}}}}[a] (79)

Now, observe that |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle is obtained from |χ⟩|\chi\rangle by taking quasiparticle 22 around quasiparticle 33, i.e. by exchanging quasiparticles 22 and 33 twice, |ψ⟩=ρ⁡(σ22)​|χ⟩|\psi\rangle=\rho\!\left({\sigma_{2}^{2}}\right)|\chi\rangle. Hence,

⟨χ|ρ⁡(σ22)|χ⟩=∫𝒟​a​ei​SC​S​[a]​Wγ1,j1​[a]​Wγ2,j2​[a]\langle\chi|\rho\!\left({\sigma_{2}^{2}}\right)|\chi\rangle=\int{\cal D}a\,e^{iS_{CS}[a]}\,{W_{{\gamma_{1}},{j_{1}}}}[a]\,{W_{{\gamma_{2}},{j_{2}}}}[a] (80)

In this way, we can compute the entries of the braiding matrices ρ⁡(σi)\rho\!\left({\sigma_{i}}\right) by computing functional integrals such as the one on the right-hand-side of (80). Note that we should normalize the state |χ⟩|\chi\rangle by computing the figure 4b, which gives its matrix element with itself.

Consider, now, the state ρ⁡(σ2)​|χ⟩\rho\!\left({\sigma_{2}}\right)|\chi\rangle, in which particles 22 and 33 are exchanged just once. It is depicted in figure 4c. Similarly, the state ρ⁡(σ2−1)​|ψ⟩\rho\!\left({\sigma_{2}^{-1}}\right)|\psi\rangle is depicted in figure 4d. From the figure, we see that

⟨χ|ρ⁡(σ2)|χ⟩\displaystyle\langle\chi|\rho\!\left({\sigma_{2}}\right)|\chi\rangle =\displaystyle= d\displaystyle d (81)
⟨χ|ρ⁡(σ2−1)|χ⟩\displaystyle\langle\chi|\rho\!\left({\sigma_{2}^{-1}}\right)|\chi\rangle =\displaystyle= d\displaystyle d (82)

since both histories contain just a single unknotted loop. Meanwhile,

⟨χ|χ⟩=d2\langle\chi|\chi\rangle=d^{2} (83)

Since the four-quasiparticle Hilbert space is two-dimensional, ρ⁡(σ2)\rho\!\left({\sigma_{2}}\right) has two eigenvalues, λ1\lambda_{1}, λ2\lambda_{2}, so that

ρ⁡(σ)−(λ1+λ2)+λ1​λ2​ρ​(σ−1)=0\rho\!\left({\sigma}\right)-\left({\lambda_{1}}+{\lambda_{2}}\right)+{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{2}}\rho\!\left({\sigma^{-1}}\right)=0 (84)

Taking the expectation value in the state |χ⟩|\chi\rangle, we find:

d−(λ1+λ2)​d2+λ1​λ2​d=0d-\left({\lambda_{1}}+{\lambda_{2}}\right){d^{2}}+{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{2}}d=0 (85)

so that

d=1+λ1​λ2λ1+λ2d=\frac{1+{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{2}}}{{\lambda_{1}}+{\lambda_{2}}} (86)

Since the braiding matrix is unitary, λ1\lambda_{1} and λ2\lambda_{2} are phases. The overall phase is unimportant for quantum computation, so we really need only a single number. In fact, this number can be obtained from self-consistency conditions [114]. However, the details of the computation of λ1\lambda_{1}, λ2\lambda_{2} within is technical and requires a careful discussion of framing; the result is [348] that λ1=−e−3πi/2(k+2){\lambda_{1}}=-e^{-3\pi i/2(k+2)}, λ2=eπ​i/2​(k+2){\lambda_{2}}=e^{\pi i/2(k+2)}. These eigenvalues are simply R012,12=λ1{R^{\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}}_{0}}~=~{\lambda_{1}}, R112,12=λ2{R^{\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}}_{1}}~=~{\lambda_{2}}. Consequently,

d=2​cos⁡(πk+2)d=2\,\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{k+2}\right) (87)

and

q−1/2ρ(σi)−q1/2ρ(σi−1)=q−q−1q^{-1/2}\rho({\sigma_{i}})-q^{1/2}{\rho\!\left(\sigma_{i}^{-1}\right)}=q-q^{-1} (88)

where q=−eπ​i/(k+2)q=-e^{\pi i/(k+2)} (see Fig. 18). Since this operator equation applies regardless of the state to which it is applied, we can apply it locally to any given part of a knot diagram to relate the amplitude to the amplitude for topologically simpler processes, as we will see below [181]. This is an example of a skein relation; in this case, it is the skein relation which defines the Jones polynomial. In arriving at this skein relation, we are retracing the connection between Wilson loops in Chern-Simons theory and knot invariants which was made in the remarkable paper [348]. In this paper, Witten showed that correlation functions of Wilson loop operators in SU(2)k Chern-Simons theory are equal to corresponding evaluations of the Jones polynomial, which is a topological invariant of knot theory [175]:

∫𝒟​a​Wγ1,12​[a]​…​Wγn,12​[a]​ei​SC​S​[a]=VL​(q)\int{\cal D}a\,W_{{\gamma_{1}},\frac{1}{2}}[a]\ldots W_{{\gamma_{n}},\frac{1}{2}}[a]\,e^{iS_{CS}[a]}=V_{L}(q) (89)

VL​(q)V_{L}(q) is the Jones polynomial associated with the link L=γ1∪…∪γnL={\gamma_{1}}\cup\ldots\cup{\gamma_{n}}, evaluated at q=−eπ​i/(k+2)q=-e^{\pi i/(k+2)} using the skein relation (88). Note that we assume here that all of the quasiparticles transform under the j=12j=\frac{1}{2} representation of S​U​(2)SU(2). The other quasiparticle types can be obtained through the fusion of several j=1/2j=1/2 quasiparticles, as we will discuss below in Section III.3.2.

III.3.2 Combinatorial Evaluation of Link Invariants and Quasiparticle Properties

The Jones polynomial [175] VL​(q)V_{L}(q) is a formal Laurent series in a variable qq which is associated to a link L=γ1∪…∪γnL={\gamma_{1}}\cup\ldots\cup{\gamma_{n}}. It can be computed recursively using (88). We will illustrate how this is done by showing how to use a skein relation to compute a related quantity called the Kauffman bracket KL​(q)K_{L}(q) [179], which differs from the Jones polynomial by a normalization:

VL​(q)=1d​(−q3/2)w⁡(L)​KL​(q)V_{L}(q)=\frac{1}{d}\,(-q^{3/2})^{w(L)}\,K_{L}(q) (90)

where w⁡(L)w(L) is the writhe of the link. (The Jones polynomial is defined for an oriented link. Given an orientation, each crossing can be assigned a sign ±1\pm 1; the writhe is the sum over all crossings of these signs.) The link LL embedded in three-dimensional space (or, rather, three-dimensional space-time in our case) is projected onto the plane. This can be done faithfully if we are careful to mark overcrossings and undercrossings. Such a projection is not unique, but the same Kauffman bracket is obtained for all possible 2​D2D projections of a knot (we will see an example of this below). An unknotted loop ○\bigcirc is given the value K○​(q)=d≡−q−q−1=2​cos⁡π/(k+2)K_{\bigcirc}(q)~=~d~\equiv~-q-q^{-1}~=~2\cos\pi/(k+2). For notational simplicity, when we draw a knot, we actually mean the Kauffman bracket associated to this knot. Hence, we write

1.0,1.0) =d\pspicture[shift=-0.4]{(}1.0,1.0) \endpspicture=\>d (91)

The disjoint union of nn unknotted loops is assigned the value dnd^{n}.

The Kauffman bracket for any given knot can be obtained recursively by repeated application of the following skein relation which relates it with the Kauffman brackets for two knots both of which have one fewer crossing according to the rule:

1.0,1.0) =q1/21.0,1.0) +q−1/21.0,1.0) \pspicture[shift=-0.4]{(}1.0,1.0) \endpspicture\>=\>q^{1/2}{\hskip-5.69046pt}\pspicture[shift=-0.4]{(}1.0,1.0) \endpspicture\;+\;q^{-1/2}{\hskip-5.69046pt}\pspicture[shift=-0.4]{(}1.0,1.0) \endpspicture (92)

With this rule, we can eliminate all crossings. At this point, we are left with a linear combination of the Kauffman brackets for various disjoint unions of unknotted loops. Adding up these contributions of the form dmd^{m} with their appropriate coefficients coming from the recursion relation (92), we obtain the Kauffman bracket for the knot with which we started.

Let us see how this works with a simple example. First, consider the two arcs which cross twice in figure 5. We will assume that these arcs continue in some arbitrary way and form closed loops. By applying the Kauffman bracket recursion relation in figure 5, we see that these arcs can be replaced by two arcs which do not cross.

In Section II.3.3, we will use these methods to evaluate some matrix elements relevant to interference experiments.

Now, let us consider the two fusion channels of a pair of quasiparticles in some more detail. When the two quasiparticles fuse to the trivial particle, as 11 and 22 did above, we can depict such a state, which we will call |0⟩|0\rangle, as 1d\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} times the state yielded by the functional integral (77) with a Wilson line which looks like ⋃\bigcup because two quasiparticles which are created as a pair out of the ground state must necessarily fuse to spin 00 if they do not braid with any other particles. (The factor 1/d1/\sqrt{d} normalizes the state.) Hence, we can project any two quasiparticles onto the j=0j=0 state by evolving them with a history which looks like:

Π0=1d1.0,1.0) {\Pi_{0}}\>=\>\frac{1}{d}{\hskip-5.69046pt}\pspicture[shift=-0.4]{(}1.0,1.0) \endpspicture (93)

On the right-hand-side of this equation, we mean a functional integral between two times t1t_{1} and t2t_{2}. The functional integral has two Wilson lines in the manner indicated pictorially. On the left-hand-side, we have suggested that evolving a state through this history can be viewed as acting on it with the projection operator Π0=|0⟩​⟨0|{\Pi_{0}}=|0\rangle\langle 0|.

However, the two quasiparticles could instead be in the state |1⟩|1\rangle, in which they fuse to form the j=1j=1 particle. Since these states must be orthogonal, ⟨0|1⟩=0\langle 0|1\rangle=0, we must get identically zero if we follow the history (93) with a history which defines a projection operator Π1\Pi_{1} onto the j=1j=1 state:

Π1=1.0,1.0) −1d1.0,1.0) {\Pi_{1}}\>=\>\pspicture[shift=-0.4]{(}1.0,1.0) \endpspicture\>-\;\frac{1}{d}{\hskip-5.69046pt}\pspicture[shift=-0.4]{(}1.0,1.0) \endpspicture (94)

It is easy to see that if this operator acts on a state which is given by a functional integral which looks like ⋃\bigcup, the result is zero.

The projection operators Π0\Pi_{0} , Π1\Pi_{1}, which are called Jones-Wenzl projection operators, project a pair of a quasiparticles onto the two natural basis states of their qubit. In other words, we do not need to introduce new types of lines in order to compute the expectation values of Wilson loops carrying j=0j=0 or j=1j=1. We can denote them with pairs of lines projected onto either of these states. Recall that a j=1/2j=1/2 loop had amplitude dd, which was the quantum dimension of a j=1/2j=1/2 particle. Using the projection operator (94), we see that a j=1j=1 loop has amplitude d2−1{d^{2}}-1 (by connecting the top of the line segments to the bottom and evaluating the Kauffman bracket). One can continue in this way to construct projection operators which project mm lines onto j=m/2j=m/2. This projection operator must be orthogonal to the j=0,1,3/2,2,…,(m−1)/2j=0,1,3/2,2,\ldots,(m-1)/2 projection operators acting on subsets of the mm lines, and this condition is sufficient to construct all of the Jones-Wenzl projection operators recursively. Similarly, the quantum dimensions can be computed through a recursion relation. At level kk, we find that quasiparticles with j>k/2j>k/2 have quantum dimensions which vanish identically (e.g. for k=1k=1, d=1d=1 so the quantum dimension of a j=1j=1 particle is d2−1=0{d^{2}}-1=0). Consequently, these quasiparticle types do not occur. Only j=0,12,…,k2j=0,\frac{1}{2},\ldots,\frac{k}{2} occur.

The entries in the FF-matrix can be obtained by graphically computing the matrix element between a state in which, for instance, 11 and 22 fuse to the vacuum and 33 and 44 fuse to the vacuum and a state in which 11 and 44 fuse to the vacuum and 22 and 33 fuse to the vacuum, which is depicted in Figure 6a. (The matrix element in this figure must be normalized by the norms of the top and bottom states to obtain the FF-matrix elements.) To compute the matrix element between a state in which 11 and 22 fuse to the vacuum and 33 and 44 fuse to the vacuum and a state in which 11 and 44 fuse to j=1j=1 and 22 and 33 fuse to j=1j=1, we must compute the diagram in Figure 6b. For k=2k=2, we find the same FF-matrix as was found for Ising anyons in Section III.2.

Let us now briefly consider the ground state properties of the SU(2)k theory on the torus. As above, we integrate the Chern-Simons Lagrangian over a 33-manifold ℳ{\cal M} with boundary Σ\Sigma, i.e. ℳ=Σ×(−∞,0]{\cal M}=\Sigma\times(-\infty,0] in order to obtain a t=0t=0 state. The boundary Σ\Sigma is the spatial slice at t=0t=0. For the torus, Σ=T2\Sigma={T^{2}}, we take ℳ{\cal M} to be the solid torus, ℳ=S1×D2{\cal M}={S^{1}}\times D^{2}, where D2D^{2} is the disk. By foliating the solid torus, we obtain earlier spatial slices. If there are no quasiparticles, then there are no Wilson lines terminating at Σ\Sigma. However, the functional integral can have Wilson loops in the body of the solid torus as in Figure 7a. These correspond to processes in the past, t<0t<0, in which a quasiparticle-quashole pair was created, taken around the meridian of the torus and annihilated. The Wilson loop can be in any of the k+1k+1 allowed representations j=0,12,…,k2j=0,\frac{1}{2},\ldots,\frac{k}{2}; in this way, we obtain k+1k+1 ground state kets on the torus (we will see momentarily that they are all linearly independent). Wilson loops around the meridian are contractible (Figure 7b), so they can be simply evaluated by taking their Kauffman bracket; they multiply the state by djd_{j}. Evidently, these Wilson loop operators are diagonal in this basis. Bras can be obtained by integrating the Chern-Simons Lagrangian over the 33-manifold ℳ′=Σ×[0,∞)=S3\S1×D2{\cal M}^{\prime}=\Sigma\times[0,\infty)={S^{3}}\backslash{S^{1}}\times D^{2}, i.e. the exterior of the torus. Wilson loops in the exterior torus are now contractible if they are parallel to a longitude but non-trivial if they are around the meridian, as in in Figure 7c. Again, we obtain k+1k+1 ground state bras in this way. The matrix elements between these bras and kets (appropriately normalized such that the matrix product of a bra with its conjugate ket is unity) are the entries in the SS-matrix, which is precisely the basis change between the longitudinal and meridinal bases. A matrix element can be computed by evaluating the corresponding picture. The a​bab entry in the SS-matrix is given by evaluating the Kauffman bracket of the picture in Figure 7d (and dividing by the normalization of the states). This figure makes the relationship between the SS-matrix and braiding clear.

Finally, we comment on the difference between SU(2)2 and Ising anyons, which we have previously described as differing only slightly from each other (See also the end of section III.5 below). The effective field theory for Ising anyons contains an additional U(1) Chern-Simons gauge field, in addition to an SU(2)2 gauge field [107, 104]. The consequences of this difference are that Θσ=e−πi/8{\Theta_{\sigma}}=e^{-\pi i/8} while Θ1/2=e−3πi/8\Theta_{1/2}=e^{-3\pi i/8}; Rσ​σ1=e−πi/8{R^{\sigma\sigma}_{1}}=e^{-\pi i/8} while R12,120=−e−3πi/8{R^{\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}}_{0}}=-e^{-3\pi i/8}; Rψσ​σ=e3​π​i/8{R^{\sigma\sigma}_{\psi}}=e^{3\pi i/8} while R112,12=eπ​i/8{R^{\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}}_{1}}=e^{\pi i/8}; [Fσσ​σ​σ]a​b=−[F1212,12,12]a​b\left[F^{\sigma\sigma\sigma}_{\sigma}\right]_{ab}=-\left[F^{\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}}_{\frac{1}{2}}\right]_{ab}. The rest of the FF-matrices are the same, as are the fusion multiplicities Na​bcN_{ab}^{c} and the SS-matrix. In other words, the basic structure of the non-Abelian statistics is the same in the two theories, but there are some minor differences in the U(1) phases which result from braiding. Both theories have threefold ground state degeneracy on the torus; the Moore-Read Pfaffian state has ground state degeneracy 66 because of an extra U(1) factor corresponding to the electrical charge degrees of freedom.

Of course, in the k=2k=2 case we have already obtained all of these results by the method of the previous subsection. However, this approach has two advantages: (1) once Witten’s result (89) and Kauffman’s recursion relation (92) are accepted, braiding matrix elements can be obtained by straightforward high school algebra; (2) the method applies to all levels kk, unlike free Majorana fermion methods which apply only to the k=2k=2 case. There is an added bonus, which is that this formalism is closely related to the techniques used to analyze lattice models of topological phases, which we discuss in a later subsection.

III.4 Chern-Simons Theory, Conformal Field Theory, and Fractional Quantum Hall States

III.4.1 The Relation between Chern-Simons Theory and Conformal Field Theory

Now, we consider Chern-Simons theory in a particular gauge, namely holomorphic gauge (to be defined below). The ground state wavefunction(s) of Chern-Simons theory can be obtained by performing the functional integral from the distant past, t=−∞t=-\infty, to time t=0t=0 as in the previous subsection:

ψ⁡[A⁡(𝐱)]=∫a⁡(𝐱,0)=A⁡(𝐱)𝒟​a​(𝐱,t)​e∫−∞0d​t​∫Σd2​x​ℒCS\psi[A({\bf x})]=\int_{a({\bf x},0)=A({\bf x})}{\cal D}a({\bf x},t)\>e^{{\int_{-\infty}^{0}}dt{\int_{\Sigma}}{d^{2}}x\>{\cal L}_{\rm CS}} (95)

For the sake of concreteness, let us consider the torus, Σ=T2\Sigma=T^{2}, for which the spacetime manifold is ℳ=(−∞,0]×T2=S1×D2{\cal M}=(-\infty,0]\times{T^{2}}={S^{1}}\times D^{2}. We assume for simplicity that there are no Wilson loops (either contained within the solid torus or terminating at the boundary). If xx and yy are coordinates on the torus (the fields will be subject to periodicity requirements), we write z=x+i​yz=x+iy. We can then change to coordinates zz, z¯{\bar{z}}, and, as usual, treat aza¯a_{z}^{\underline{a}} and az¯a¯a_{\bar{z}}^{\underline{a}} as independent variables. Then, we take the holomorphic gauge, az¯a¯=0a_{\bar{z}}^{\underline{a}}=0. The field az¯a¯{a_{\bar{z}}^{\underline{a}}} only appears in the action linearly, so the functional integral over az¯a¯{a_{\bar{z}}^{\underline{a}}} may be performed, yielding a δ\delta-function:

∫D​a​ek4​π​∫D2×S1ϵμ​ν​λ​(aμa​∂νaλa+23​fa​b​c​aμa​aνb​aλc)=\displaystyle\int Da\>{e^{\frac{k}{4\pi}\int_{{D^{2}}\times S^{1}}\epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda}\left({a_{\mu}^{a}}{\partial_{\nu}}{a_{\lambda}^{a}}+\frac{2}{3}{f_{abc}}{a_{\mu}^{a}}{a_{\nu}^{b}}{a_{\lambda}^{c}}\right)}}= (96)
∫D​ai​δ​(fi​ja¯)​ek4​π​∫D2×S1ϵi​j​aia​∂z¯aja\displaystyle\int D{a_{i}}\,\delta(f_{ij}^{\underline{a}})\,{e^{\frac{k}{4\pi}\int_{{D^{2}}\times S^{1}}\epsilon^{ij}{a_{i}^{a}}{\partial_{\bar{z}}}{a_{j}^{a}}}} (97)

where i,j=t,zi,j=t,z. Here fi​ja¯=p​a​r​t​i​a​li​aja¯−p​a​r​t​i​a​lj​aia¯+i​ϵa¯​b¯​c¯​aia¯​ajb¯f_{ij}^{\underline{a}}={partial_{i}}a_{j}^{\underline{a}}-{partial_{j}}a_{i}^{\underline{a}}+i\epsilon_{{\underline{a}}{\underline{b}}{\underline{c}}}a_{i}^{\underline{a}}a_{j}^{\underline{b}} are the spatial components of the field strength. There are no other cubic terms in the action once az¯a_{\bar{z}} has been eliminated (as is the case in any such gauge in which one of the components of the gauge field vanishes). The constraint imposed by the δ\delta-function can be solved by taking

aia=∂iU​U−1{a_{i}^{a}}={\partial_{i}}U\,{U^{-1}} (98)

where UU is a single-valued function taking values in the Lie group. Substituting this into the right-hand-side of (96), we find that the action which appears in the exponent in the functional integral takes the form

S\displaystyle S =\displaystyle= k4​π​∫D2×S1ϵi​j​tr​(∂iU​U−1​∂z¯(∂jU​U−1))\displaystyle{\frac{k}{4\pi}\int_{{D^{2}}\times S^{1}}\epsilon^{ij}\text{tr}\left({\partial_{i}}U\,{U^{-1}}{\partial_{\bar{z}}}\left({\partial_{j}}U\,{U^{-1}}\right)\right)} (99)

tr(∂iUU−1∂jU∂z¯U−1)]\displaystyle{\hskip 76.82234pt}\text{tr}\left({\partial_{i}}U\,{U^{-1}}{\partial_{j}}U\,{\partial_{\bar{z}}}{U^{-1}}\right)\biggr]
=\displaystyle= k4​π∫D2×S1ϵi​j[∂jtr(∂iU−1∂z¯U)+\displaystyle\frac{k}{4\pi}\int_{{D^{2}}\times S^{1}}\epsilon^{ij}\biggl[{\partial_{j}}\text{tr}\left({\partial_{i}}\,{U^{-1}}{\partial_{\bar{z}}}U\right)\>+ (103)
tr(∂iUU−1∂jU∂z¯U−1)]\displaystyle{\hskip 76.82234pt}\text{tr}\left({\partial_{i}}U\,{U^{-1}}{\partial_{j}}U\,{\partial_{\bar{z}}}{U^{-1}}\right)\biggr]
=\displaystyle= k4​π​∫T2tr​(∂zU−1​∂z¯U)+\displaystyle\frac{k}{4\pi}\int_{T^{2}}\text{tr}\left({\partial_{z}}{U^{-1}}{\partial_{\bar{z}}}U\right)\>+ (104)
k12​π​∫D2×S1ϵμ​ν​λ​tr​(∂μU​U−1​∂νU​U−1​∂λU​U−1)\displaystyle{\hskip-19.91684pt}\frac{k}{12\pi}\int_{{D^{2}}\times S^{1}}\epsilon^{\mu\nu\lambda}\text{tr}\left({\partial_{\mu}}U\,{U^{-1}}{\partial_{\nu}}U\,{U^{-1}}\,{\partial_{\lambda}}U\,{U^{-1}}\right) (105)

The Jacobian which comes from the δ\delta-function δ⁡(fi​ja¯)\delta(f_{ij}^{\underline{a}}) is cancelled by that associated with the change of integration variable from D​aDa to D​UDU. In the final line, the first term has been integrated by parts while the second term, although it appears to be an integral over the 3​D3D manifold, only depends on the boundary values of UU [339, 347]. This is the Wess-Zumino-Witten (WZW) action. What we learn from (105) then, is that, in a particular gauge, the ground state wavefunction of 2+12+1-D Chern-Simons theory can be viewed as the partition function of a 2+02+0-dimensional WZW model.

For positive integer kk, the WZW model is a 2​D2D conformal field theory which, in the SU(2) case, has Virasoro central charge c=c¯=3​kk+2c={\bar{c}}=\frac{3k}{k+2}. (For a brief review of some of the basics of conformal field theory, see appendix A and references therein.) However, in computing properties of the Chern-Simons theory from which we have derived it, we will couple only to az=∂zU⋅U−1a_{z}={\partial_{z}}U\cdot U^{-1}; i.e. only to the holomorphic or right-moving sector of the theory. Thus, it is the chiral WZW model which controls the ground state wavefunction(s) of Chern-Simons theory.

If we were to follow the same strategy to calculate the Chern-Simons ground state wavefunction with Wilson lines or punctures present, then we would end up with a correlation function of operators in the chiral WZW model transforming under the corresponding representations of SU(2). (Strictly speaking, it is not a correlation function, but a conformal block, which is a chiral building block for a correlation function. While correlation functions are single-valued, conformal blocks have the non-trivial monodromy properties which we need, as is discussed in appendix A.) Therefore, following [348, 86], we have mapped the problem of computing the ground state wavefunction (in 2+02+0-dimensions) of Chern-Simons theory, which is a topological theory with a gap, to the problem of computing a correlation function in the chiral WZW model (in 1+11+1-dimensions), which is a critical theory. This is a bit peculiar since one theory is gapped while the other is gapless. However, the gapless degrees of freedom of the WZW model for the t=0t=0 spatial slice are pure gauge degrees of freedom for the corresponding Chern-Simons theory. (In the very similar situation of a surface Σ\Sigma with boundary, however, the corresponding conformally-invariant 1+11+1-D theory describes the actual dynamical excitations of the edge of the system, as we discuss in section III.5.) Only the topological properties of the chiral WZW conformal blocks are physically meaningful for us.

More complicated topological states with multiple Chern-Simons fields and, possibly, Higgs fields [107, 106, 104] correspond in a similar way to other chiral rational conformal field theories which are obtained by tensoring or cosetting WZW models. (RCFTs are those CFTs which have a finite number of primary fields – see appendix A for the definition of a primary field – under some extended chiral algebra which envelopes the Virasoro algebra; a Kac-Moody algebra in the WZW case; and, possibly, other symmetry generators.) Consequently, it is possible to use the powerful algebraic techniques of rational conformal field theory to compute the ground state wavefunctions of a large class of topological states of matter. The quasiparticles of the topological state correspond to the primary fields of the chiral RCFT. (It is a matter of convenience whether one computes correlation functions with a primary field or one of its descendants since their topological properties are the same. This is a freedom which can be exploited, as we describe below.)

The conformal blocks of an RCFT have one property which is particularly useful for us, namely they are holomorphic functions of the coordinates. This makes them excellent candidate wavefunctions for quantum Hall states. We identify primary fields with the quasiparticles of the quantum Hall state, and compute the corresponding conformal block. However, there is one important issue which must be resolved: a quantum Hall wavefunction is normally viewed as a wavefunction for electrons (the quasiparticle positions, by contrast, are usually viewed merely as some collective coordinates specifying a given excited state). Where are the electrons in our RCFT? Electrons have trivial braiding properties. When one electron is taken around another, the wavefunction is unchanged, except for a phase change which is an odd integral multiple of 2​π2\pi. More importantly, when any quasiparticle is taken around an electron, the wavefunction is unchanged apart from a phase change which is an integral multiple of 2​π2\pi. Therefore, the electron must be a descendant of the identity. In other words, the RCFT must contain a fermionic operator by which we can extend the chiral algebra. This new symmetry generator is essentially the electron creation operator – which is, therefore, a descendant of the identity under its own action. Not all RCFTs have such an operator in their spectrum, so this is a strong constraint on RCFTs which can describe quantum Hall states. If we are interested, instead, in a quantum Hall state of bosons, as could occur with ultra-cold bosonic atoms in a rotating optical trap [64], then the RCFT must contain a bosonic field by which we can extend the chiral algebra.

An RCFT correlation function of NeN_{e} electron operators therefore corresponds to the Chern-Simons ground state wavefunction with NeN_{e} topologically-trivial Wilson lines. From a purely topological perspective, such a wavefunction is just as good as a wavefunction with no Wilson lines, so the Wilson lines would seem superfluous. However, if the descendant field which represents the electron operator is chosen cleverly, then the wavefunction with NeN_{e} Wilson lines may be a ‘good’ trial wavefunction for electrons in the quantum Hall regime. Indeed, in some cases, one finds that these trial wavefunctions are the exact quantum Hall ground states of simple model Hamiltonians [233, 31, 336, 270, 142, 9, 296]. In the study of the quantum Hall effect, however, a wavefunction is ‘good’ if it is energetically favorable for a realistic Hamiltonian, which is beyond the scope of the underlying Chern-Simons theory, which itself only knows about braiding properties. It is unexpected good luck that the trial wavefunctions obtained from Chern-Simons theory are often found to be ‘good’ from this energetic perspective, which is a reflection of how highly constrained quantum Hall wavefunctions are, and how central these braiding properties are to their physics. We emphasize, however, that a wavefunction obtained in this way will not be the exact ground state wavefunction for electrons with Coulomb interactions. In some cases it might not even have particularly high overlap with the ground state wavefunction, or have good energetics. The one thing which it does capture is the topological structure of a particular universality class.

III.4.2 Quantum Hall Wavefunctions from Conformal Field Theory

Ideally, the logic which would lead us to a particular RCFT would be as follows, as displayed in Fig. 8. One begins with the experimental observation of the quantized Hall effect at some filling fraction ν\nu (shown at the top). We certainly know that the Hamiltonian for the system is simply that of 2D electrons in a magnetic field, and at the bottom, we know the form of the low energy theory should be of Chern-Simons form. One would like to be able to “integrate out” high energy degrees of freedom directly to obtain the low-energy theory. Given the low-energy Chern-Simons effective field theory, one can pass to the associated RCFT, as described above. With the RCFT in hand, one can construct wavefunctions, as we will describe below. Indeed, such a procedure has been explicitly achieved for Abelian quantum Hall states [362, 218]. In some special non-Abelian cases, progress in this direction has been made [331, 333].

For most non-Abelian theories, however, the situation is not so simple. The RCFT is usually obtained through inspired guesswork [233, 31, 270, 9, 51, 298]. One may try to justify it ex post facto by solving for the properties of quasiholes of a system with some unrealistic (e.g. involving 33-body or higher interactions) but soluble Hamiltonian. The degeneracy can be established by counting [247, 269, 266]. The braiding matrices can be obtained by numerically computing the Berry integrals for the given wavefunctions [320] or by using their connection to conformal field theory to deduce them [233, 247, 147, 299]. One can then deduce the Chern-Simons effective field theory of the state either from the quasiparticle properties or from the associated conformal field theory with which both it and the wavefunctions are connected.

We now show how such wavefunctions can be constructed through some examples. In appendix A, we review some of the rudiments of conformal field theory.

(a) Wavefunctions from CFTs: Our goal is to construct a LLL FQH wavefunction Ψ⁡(z1,…,zN)\Psi(z_{1},\ldots,z_{N}) which describes an electron fluid in a circular droplet centered at the origin. Ψ\Psi must be a homogeneous antisymmetric analytic function of the ziz_{i}s, independent of the z¯i{\bar{z}}_{i}s apart from the Gaussian factor, which we will frequently ignore (see Sec. II.3.1). If we consider the FQHE of bosons, we would need Ψ\Psi to instead be symmetric. The filling fraction ν\nu of a FQH wavefunction Ψ\Psi is given by ν=N/NΦ\nu=N/N_{\Phi} where NN is the number of electrons and NΦN_{\Phi} is the number of flux quanta penetrating the droplet [261]. In the LLL, NΦN_{\Phi} is given by the highest power of zz occurring in Ψ\Psi.

We will also frequently need the fact that in an incompressible state of filling fraction ν\nu, multiplying a wavefuncton by a factor ∏i(zi−w)m{\prod_{i}}({z_{i}}-w)^{m} pushes a charge ν​m\nu m away from the point ww. This can be understood [202] as insertion of mm flux quanta at the point ww, which, via Faraday’s law creates an azimuthal electric field, which, then, via the Hall conductivity transfers charge ν​m\nu m away from the point ww.

Our strategy will be to choose a particular chiral RCFT, pick an “electron” field ψe\psi_{e} in this theory (which, by the reasoning given above, must be a fermionic generator of the extended chiral algebra of the theory), and write a ground state trial wavefunction Ψgs\Psi_{\rm gs} for NN electrons as

Ψgs=⟨ψe​(z1)​…​ψe​(zN)⟩\Psi_{\rm gs}=\langle\,\psi_{e}(z_{1})\ldots\psi_{e}(z_{N})\,\rangle (106)

The field ψe\psi_{e} must be fermionic since the quantum Hall wavefunction on the left-hand-side must be suitable for electrons. Not all RCFTs have such a field in their spectrum, so this requirement constrains our choice. This requirement also ensures that we will obtain a wavefunction which has no branch cuts; in particular, there will only be one conformal block on the right-hand-side of (106). We must do a little more work in choosing ψe\psi_{e} so that there are no poles either on the right-hand-side of (106). As discussed above, the correlation function on the right-hand-side of (106) is a ground state wavefunction of Chern-Simons theory with NeN_{e} trivial topological charges at fixed positions z1,z2,…,zNe{z_{1}},{z_{2}},\ldots,{z_{N_{e}}}.

Of course, there isn’t a unique choice of RCFT, even at a given filling fraction. Therefore, there are different fractional quantum Hall states which can be constructed in this way. Which fractional quantum Hall state is actually observed at a particular ν\nu is determined by comparing the energies of the various possible competing ground states. Having a good wavefunction is, by itself, no guarantee that this wavefunction actually describes the physical system. Only a calculation of its energy gives real evidence that it is better than other possible states.

The reason for introducing this complex machinery simply to construct a wavefunction becomes clearer when we consider quasihole wavefunctions, which are Chern-Simons ground state wavefunctions with NeN_{e} trivial topological charges and Nq​hN_{qh} non-trivial topological charges. In general, there are many possible quasihole operators, corresponding to the different primary fields of the theory, so we must really consider Nq​h​1,Nq​h​2,…​Nq​h​mN_{qh1},N_{qh2},\ldots N_{qhm} numbers of quasiholes if there are mm primary fields. Each different primary field corresponds to a different topologically-distinct type of “defect” in the ground state. (As in the case of electrons, we are free to choose a descendant field in place of the corresponding primary field since the two have identical topological properties although the wavefunction generated by a descendant will be different from that generated by its primary.) Let us suppose that we focus attention on a particular type of quasiparticle which, in most cases, will be the quasiparticle of minimal electrical charge. Then we can write a wavefunction with quasiholes at positions w1,…,wMw_{1},\ldots,w_{M} as

Ψ⁡(w1​…​wM)=⟨ψq​h​(w1)​…​ψq​h​(wM)​ψe​(z1)​…​ψe​(zN)⟩\Psi(w_{1}\!\ldots w_{M}\!)\!=\!\langle\psi_{qh}(w_{1})\ldots\psi_{qh}(w_{M})\,\,\,\psi_{e}(z_{1})\ldots\psi_{e}(z_{N})\rangle (107)

where ψq​h\psi_{qh} is the corresponding primary field. Since ψq​h\psi_{qh} is a primary field and ψe\psi_{e} is a descendant of the identity, we are guaranteed that ψq​h\psi_{qh} and ψe\psi_{e} are local with respect to each other, i.e. taking one field around can only produce a phase which is a multiple of 2​π2\pi. Consequently, the wavefunction Ψ\Psi remains analytic in the electron coordinates ziz_{i} even after the fields ψq​h​(w1)​…​ψq​h​(wM)\psi_{qh}(w_{1})\ldots\psi_{qh}(w_{M}) have been inserted into the correlation function.

One important feature of the conformal block on the right-hand-side of (107) is that ψq​h​(wa)\psi_{qh}(w_{a}) and ψe​(zi)\psi_{e}(z_{i}) are on roughly the same footing – they are both fields in some conformal field theory (or, equivalently, they are both fixed sources coupled to the Chern-Simons gauge field). However, when intepreted as a wavefunction on the left-hand-side of (107), the electron coordinates ziz_{i} are the variables for which the wavefunction gives a probability amplitude while the quasihole coordinates waw_{a} are merely some parameters in this wavefunction. If we wished to normalize the wavefunction differently, we could multiply by an arbitrary function of the waw_{a}s. However, the particular normalization which is given by the right-hand-side of (107) is particularly convenient, as we will see momentarily. Note that since the quasihole positions wjw_{j} are merely parameters in the wavefunction, the wavefunction need not be analytic in these coordinates.

(b) Quasiparticle Braiding: The branch cuts in quasihole positions waw_{a} are symptoms of the fact that there may be a vector space of conformal blocks corresponding to the right-hand-side of (107). In such a case, even when the quasihole positions are fixed, there are several possible linearly independent wavefunctions. These multiple degenerate states are necessary for non-Abelian statistics, and they will generically mix when the quasiholes are dragged around each other.

However, there is still a logical gap in the above reasoning. The wavefunctions produced by an RCFT have the correct braiding properties for the corresponding Chern-Simons ground state wavefunction built into them through their explicit monodromy properties. As a result of the branch cuts in the conformal blocks as a function of the waw_{a}s, when one quasihole is taken around another, the wavefunction Ψα\Psi^{\alpha} transforms into Mα​β​ΨβM^{\alpha\beta}\Psi^{\beta}, where the index α=1,2,…,g\alpha=1,2,\ldots,g runs over the gg different degenerate nn-quasihole states. However, when viewed as quantum Hall wavefunctions, their quasiparticle braiding properties are a combination of their explicit monodromy and the Berry matrix which is obtained from:

ei​γα​β=𝒫​exp⁡(∮d​w→​⟨Ψα|∇w→|Ψβ⟩)e^{i\gamma_{\alpha\beta}}={\cal P}\exp\left(\oint d{\vec{w}}\Bigl\langle\Psi^{\alpha}\Bigl|\nabla_{\vec{w}}\Bigr|\Psi^{\beta}\Bigr\rangle\right) (108)

where Ψα\Psi^{\alpha}, α=1,2,…,g\alpha=1,2,\ldots,g are the gg different degenerate nn-quasihole states and P is the path ordering symbol. In this equation, the ziz_{i}s are integrated over in order to compute the inner product, but the waw_{a}s are held fixed, except for the one which is taken around some loop.

Strictly speaking, the effect of braiding is to transform a state according to Ψα→ei​γα​β​Mβ​γ​Ψγ\Psi^{\alpha}\rightarrow e^{i\gamma_{\alpha\beta}}M^{\beta\gamma}\Psi^{\gamma}. By changing the normalization of the wavefunction, we can alter ei​γα​βe^{i\gamma_{\alpha\beta}} and Mβ​γM^{\beta\gamma}. Only the product of the two matrices on the right-hand-side of this equation is gauge invariant and physically meaningful. When we presume that the braiding properties of this wavefunction are given by those of the corresponding CFT and Chern-Simons theory, we take it to be equal to Mβ​γM^{\beta\gamma} and ignore ei​γα​βe^{i\gamma_{\alpha\beta}}. This can only be correct if γα​β\gamma_{\alpha\beta} vanishes up to a geometric phase proportional to the area for a wavefunction given by a CFT conformal block. In the case of the Laughlin states, it can be verified that this is indeed correct by repeating the the Arovas, Schrieffer, Wilczek calculation [11] with the Laughlin state normalized according to the quasihole position dependence given by the corresponding CFT (see below) [31]. This calculation rests upon the plasma analogy originally introduced by Laughlin in his seminal work [202]. For other, more complex states, it is more difficult to compute the Berry matrix. A version of a plasma analogy for the MR Pfaffian state was constructed in 147; one could thereby verify the vanishing of the Berry matrix for a two-quasihole state and, with some further assumptions, for four and higher multiquasihole states. A direct evaluation of the integral in (108) by the Monte-Carlo method [320] established that it vanishes for MR Pfaffian quasiholes. The effect of Landau level mixing on statistics has also been studied [294]. Although there has not been a complete proof that the CFT-Chern-Simons braiding rules are identical to those of the wavefunction, when it is interpreted as an electron wavefunction (i.e. there has not been a complete proof that (108) vanishes when the wavefunction is a CFT conformal block), there is compelling evidence for the MR Pfaffian state, and it is almost certainly true for many other states as well. We will, therefore, take it as a given that we can simply read off the braiding properties of the wavefunctions which we construct below.

(c) The Laughlin State: We now consider wavefunctions generated by perhaps the simplest CFT, the chiral boson. We suppose that the chiral boson has compactification radius m\sqrt{m}, so that ϕ≡ϕ+2​π​m\phi\equiv\phi+2\pi\sqrt{m}. The U(1) Kac-Moody algebra and enveloping Virasoro algebra can be extended by the symmetry generator ei​ϕ​me^{i\phi\sqrt{m}}. Since the dimension of this operator is m/2m/2, it is fermionic for mm odd and bosonic for even mm. The primary fields of this extended chiral algebra are of the form ei​n​ϕ/me^{in\phi/\sqrt{m}}, with n=0,1,…,m−1n=0,1,\ldots,m-1. They are all of the fields which are not descendants and are local with respect to ei​ϕ​me^{i\phi\sqrt{m}} (and to the Kac-Moody and Virasoro generators), as may be seen from the operator product expansion (OPE) (see Appendix A):

ei​ϕ​(z)​m​ei​n​ϕ​(0)/m∼zn​ei⁡(n+m)​ϕ​(0)/m+…e^{i\phi(z)\sqrt{m}}\,e^{in\phi(0)/\sqrt{m}}\sim{z^{n}}\,e^{i(n+m)\phi(0)/\sqrt{m}}+\ldots (109)

When zz is taken around the origin, the right-hand-side is unchanged. It is convenient to normalize the U⁡(1)U(1) current as j=1m​∂ϕj=\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\partial\phi; then the primary field ei​n​ϕ/me^{in\phi/\sqrt{m}} has charge n/mn/m. We take ψe=ei​ϕ​m{\psi_{e}}=e^{i\phi\sqrt{m}} as our electron field (which has charge 1) and consider the resulting ground state wavefunction according to Eq. 106. Using Eq. 178 we find

Ψgs=⟨ψe​(z1)​…​ψe​(zN)⟩=∏i<j​(zi−zj)m\Psi_{\rm gs}=\langle\psi_{e}(z_{1})\ldots\psi_{e}(z_{N})\rangle={\mbox{$\prod_{i<j}$}}\,\,\,(z_{i}-z_{j})^{m} (110)

It is now clear why we have chosen this CFT: to have Ψgs\Psi_{\rm gs} given by correlators of a vertex operator of the form ei​α​ϕe^{i\alpha\phi} analytic (no branch cuts or poles) we must have α2=m\alpha^{2}=m a nonnegative integer, and mm must be odd to obtain an antisymmetric wavefunction (or even for symmetric). We recognize Ψgs\Psi_{\rm gs} as the ν=1/m\nu=1/m Laughlin wavefunction. The astute reader will notice that the correlator in Eq. 110 actually violates the neutrality condition discussed in Appendix A and so it should actually have zero value. One fix for this problem is to insert into the correlator (by hand) a neutralizing vertex operator at infinity e−i​N​ϕ​(z=∞)​me^{-iN\phi(z=\infty)\sqrt{m}} which then makes Eq. 110 valid (up to a contant factor). Another approach is to insert an operator that smears the neutralizing background over the entire system [233]. This approach also conveniently results in the neglected Gaussian factors reappearing! We will ignore these neutralizing factors for simplicity. From now on, we will drop the Gaussian factors from quantum Hall wavefunctions, with the understanding that they result from including a smeared neutralizing background.

The quasihole operator must be a primary field; the primary field of minimum charge is ei​ϕ/me^{i\phi/\sqrt{m}}. Using Eq. 178, Eq. 107 yields

Ψ⁡(w1,…,wM)=Πi<jM(wi−wj)1/m​Πi=1NΠj=1M(zi−wj)​Ψgs\Psi(w_{1},\ldots,w_{M}\!)\!=\!\mathop{\Pi}^{M}_{i<j}(w_{i}-w_{j})^{1/m}\mathop{\Pi}_{i=1}^{N}\mathop{\Pi}_{j=1}^{M}(z_{i}-w_{j})\Psi_{\rm gs} (111)

As mentioned above, the factor ∏j​(zj−w)\mbox{$\prod_{j}$}\,(z_{j}-w) “pushes” charge away from the position ww leaving a hole of charge precisely Q=+e/mQ=+e/m. The first term on the right of Eq. 111 results from the fusion of quasihole operators with each other, and explicitly shows the fractional statistics of the quasiholes. Adiabatically taking two quasiholes around each other results in a fractional phase of 2​π/m2\pi/m. As promised above, this statistical term appears automatically in the wavefunction given by this CFT!

(d) Moore-Read Pfaffian State:

In the Ising CFT (see Appendix A), we might try to use ψe​(z)=ψ​(z)\psi_{e}(z)=\psi(z) as the electron field [233]. The ψ\psi fields can fuse together in pairs to give the identity (since ψ×ψ=𝟏\psi\times\psi=\bf 1) so long as there are an even number of fields. However, when we take two ψ\psi fields close to each other, the OPE tells us that

limzi→zjψ⁡(zi)​ψ​(zj)∼𝟏/(zi−zj)\lim_{z_{i}\rightarrow z_{j}}\psi(z_{i})\psi(z_{j})\sim{\bf 1}/(z_{i}-z_{j}) (112)

which diverges as zi→zj{z_{i}}\rightarrow{z_{j}} and is therefore unacceptable as a wavefunction. To remedy this problem, we tensor the Ising CFT with the chiral boson CFT. There is now an operator ψ​ei​ϕ​m\psi\,e^{i\phi\sqrt{m}} by which we can extend the chiral algebra. (If mm is even, this symmetry generator is fermionic; if mm is odd, it is bosonic.) As before, we will take this symmetry generator to be our electron field. The corresponding primary fields are of the form ei​n​ϕ/me^{in\phi/\sqrt{m}}, σ​ei⁡(2​n+1)​ϕ/2​m\sigma\,e^{i(2n+1)\phi/2\sqrt{m}}, and ψ​ei​n​ϕ/m\psi\,e^{in\phi/\sqrt{m}}, where n=0,1,…,m−1n=0,1,\ldots,m-1. Again, these are determined by the requirement of locality with respect to the generators of the chiral algebra, i.e. that they are single-valued when taken around a symmetry generator, in particular the elecron field ψ​ei​ϕ​m\psi\,e^{i\phi\sqrt{m}}. For instance,

ψ⁡(z)​ei​ϕ​(z)​m⋅σ⁡(0)​ei⁡(2​n+1)​ϕ​(0)/2​m∼z−1/2σ(0)zn+1/2ei⁡(2​(n+m)+1)​ϕ​(0)/m+…=zn​σ​(0)​ei⁡(2​(n+m)+1)​ϕ​(0)/m\psi(z)\,e^{i\phi(z)\sqrt{m}}\cdot\sigma(0)\,e^{i(2n+1)\phi(0)/2\sqrt{m}}\sim\\ z^{-1/2}\sigma(0)\,z^{n+1/2}e^{i{(2(n+m)+1)}\phi(0)/\sqrt{m}}+\ldots\\ =z^{n}\sigma(0)\,e^{i{(2(n+m)+1)}\phi(0)/\sqrt{m}} (113)

and similarly for the other primary fields.

Using our new symmetry generator as the electron field, we obtain the ground state wavefunction according to Eq. 106:

Ψgs=⟨ψ⁡(z1)​…​ψ​(zN)⟩​∏i<j​(zi−zj)m=Pf​(1zi−zj)​∏i<j​(zi−zj)m\Psi_{\rm gs}=\langle\psi(z_{1})\ldots\psi(z_{N})\rangle\,\,\,\mbox{$\prod_{i<j}$}(z_{i}-z_{j})^{m}\\ =\text{Pf}\!\left(\frac{1}{z_{i}-z_{j}}\right)\,\mbox{$\prod_{i<j}$}(z_{i}-z_{j})^{m} (114)

(See, e.g. 73 for the calculation of this correlation function.) Again, mm odd gives an antisymmetric wavefunction and mm even gives a symmetric wavefunction. For m=2m=2 (and even NN), Eq. 114 gives precisely the Moore-Read Pfaffian wavefunction (Eq. 56 with g=1/zg=1/z and two Jastrow factors attached).

To determine the filling fraction of our newly constructed wavefunction, we need only look at the exponent of the Jastrow factor in Eq. 114. Recall that the filling fraction is determined by the highest power of any zz (See III.4.1 above). There are m⁡(N−1)m(N-1) factors of z1z_{1} in the Jastrow factor. The Pfaffian has a factor of z1z_{1} in the denominator, so the highest power of z1z_{1} is m⁡(N−1)−1m(N-1)-1. However, in the thermodynamic limit, the number of factors scales as m​NmN. Thus the filling fraction is ν=1/m\nu=1/m.

We now consider quasihole operators. As in the Laughlin case we might consider the primary fields ψq​h=ei​n​ϕ/m\psi_{qh}=e^{in\phi/\sqrt{m}}. Similar arguments as in the Laughlin case show that the n=1n=1 case generates precisely the Laughlin quasihole of charge Q=+e/mQ=+e/m. However we have other options for our quasihole which have smaller electrical charge. The primary field σ​ei​ϕ/2​m\sigma\,e^{i\phi/2\sqrt{m}} has charge Q=+e/2mQ=+e/2m. We then obtain the wavefunction according to Eq. 107

Ψ(w1,…,wM)=⟨σ(w1)…σ(wm)ψ(z1)…ψ(zN)⟩×\displaystyle\!\!\!\!\!\Psi(\!w_{1},\ldots,w_{M}\!)\!=\!\langle\sigma(w_{1})\ldots\sigma(w_{m})\psi(z_{1})\ldots\psi(z_{N})\rangle\times
Πi<jM(wi−wj)1/2​m​Πi=1NΠj=1M(zi−wj)1/2​Πi<jN(zi−zj)m\displaystyle\!\!\!\!\!\!\mathop{\Pi}^{M}_{i<j}(w_{i}-w_{j})^{1/2m}\mathop{\Pi}_{i=1}^{N}\mathop{\Pi}_{j=1}^{M}(z_{i}-w_{j})^{1/2}\mathop{\Pi}_{i<j}^{N}(z_{i}-z_{j})^{m}~~ (115)

Using the fusion rules of the σ\sigma fields (See Eq. 9, as well as Fig. 22 and Table 2 in Appendix A), we see that it is impossible to obtain 𝟏\bf 1 from an odd number of σ\sigma fields. We conclude that quasiholes ψq​h\psi_{qh} can only occur in pairs. Let us then consider the simplest case of two quasiholes. If there is an even number of electrons, the ψ\psi fields fuse in pairs to form 𝟏\bf 1, and the remaining two quasiholes must fuse to form 𝟏\bf 1 also. As discussed in Eq. 174 the OPE of the two σ\sigma fields will then have a factor of (w1−w2)−1/8(w_{1}-w_{2})^{-1/8}. In addition, the fusion of the two vertex operators ei​ϕ/2​me^{i\phi/2\sqrt{m}} results in the first term in the second line of Eq. 115, (w1−w2)1/(4​m)(w_{1}-w_{2})^{1/(4m)}. Thus the phase accumulated by taking the two quasiholes around each other is −2π/8+2π/4m-2\pi/8+2\pi/4m.

On the other hand, with an odd number of electrons in the system, the ψ\psi’s fuse in pairs, but leave one unpaired ψ\psi. The two σ\sigma’s must then fuse to form a ψ\psi which can then fuse with the unpaired ψ\psi to give the identity. (See Eq. 174). In this case, the OPE of the two σ\sigma fields will give a factor of (w1−w2)3/8(w_{1}-w_{2})^{3/8}. Thus the phase accumulated by taking the two quasiholes around each other is 6​π/8+2​π/4​m6\pi/8+2\pi/4m.

In the language of section III.2 above, when there is an even number of electrons in the system, all of these are paired and the fermion orbital shared by the quasiholes is unoccupied. When an odd electron is added, it ‘occupies’ this orbital, although the fermion orbital is neutral and the electron is charged (we can think of the electrons’ charge as being screened by the superfluid).

When there are many quasiholes, they may fuse together in many different ways.
